speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: PHOTESTS AGAINST CURTAILMENT OP TRAIN SERVICE BETWEEN HARDISTY AND CAMROSE
speechtext: I desire to direct a question to the Minister of Railways based on very strong protests I have received from boards of trade and other bodies along the line of the Canadian Pacific railway from Hardisty to Camrose. The protest is in regard to the action of that company in arbitrarily cutting off the Hardisty local, so-called, which has served that district for over twenty-five years. I should like to ask the minister if there is anything he can do in this matter, either through his position as Minister of Railways or through the board of railway commissioners.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
maintopic: CANADIAN PACIFIC RAILWAY
subtopic: PHOTESTS AGAINST CURTAILMENT OP TRAIN SERVICE BETWEEN HARDISTY AND CAMROSE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman himself protested to me in this regard a few days ago, and I have had as well a number of protests such as he has had. I should like to point out that the Canadian Pacific Railway, like the Canadian National Railways, is making a good many restrictions in its service for economic reasons, because of the business depression. Both railways are making these restrictions for that reason, and I am receiving protests
from all over the country particularly with regard to the Canadian National Railways, but occasionally with regard to the Canadian Pacific Railway, as in this case.
I may as well make this statement now: The only redress the people have is to appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners. I have no control at all over either the Canadian National Railways or the Canadian Pacific Railway in regard to these restrictions of service. 1 made special inquiries of the Board of Railway Commissioners in regard to the matter, and they tell me that generally there is a notice posted by the railway company giving ten days notice as to the changes which are to be made. Then if the people wish to protest, as in the present case, if they take it up with the Board of Railway Commissioners the board immediately goes into the question and, if they think it is worth further consideration, they request the railway to hold up the change pending final determination.
They can do that at any time they choose, and if, following that investigation, they find that, in the interests of the public, the change should not be made, they can refuse to permit it.
I am sorry I cannot do anything in the matter. My hon. friend should direct the protests, as I have already directed them, to the Board of Railway Commissioners. The decision is entirely in their hands.

Agricultural Conditions

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext: ["Order. It is now nine o'clock, and the house will revert to the motion under consideration at six o'clock."]

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in resuming my remarks on the motion of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), with reference to agricultural conditions throughout the country, may I point out that previous speakers have almost all laid stress on the conditions prevailing in western Canada. At the outset of my remarks, the other day, I stated that agricultural industry is an important factor in certain sections of Canada, namely Ontario and Quebec, and that it calls for the consideration of this government which seems, on the contrary, to look upon farming as a trifling matter. My statement is based on the silence of hon. members on your right, Sir, and their refusal to state to the house the policy which the government intend to follow as regards agriculture and which, we on this side of the house, are entitled to expect and know so as to carry on this debate with an adequate knowledge of the facts.
The opposition and the Canadian people, however, have in vain tried to get the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) to make that statement. We have therefore, sir, a perfect right to surmise and form an opinion based on the speeches delivered in public by certain cabinet ministers, since they have assumed office. It further give us the right and the opportunity to criticize the present government's attitude, in the hope that they will break silence and make a clear-cut statement which is anxiously awaited by the Canadian people.
In support of my contentions, I have already pointed out to this house the fact that certain hon. cabinet ministers, representing agricultural ri dings, never mentioned in their speeches, a single measure bearing on the welfare of the farming community. I shall add that this aloofness towards the farming class seems to be reflected in a speech delivered by the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) who represents the agricultural riding of Laval-Two Mountains. Let me quote extracts from that speech in support of my contention. The newspaper "La Presse" on march 24, 1931, reports that the hon. Postmaster, after having according to custom, highly complimented the ladies, after having commented at length on the part which women play in society, home education of youth and the sound motherly advices which make for happiness and wisdom; after dealing with certain economical questions of ours and explained- his opposition to women suffrage when he was leader of the opposition in Quebec, after having narrated historical facts; after having expressed the wish of speaking of the seventeenth century, of Madame de Sevigne and Madame de
Maintenon, quoted the works of Rivarol and Voltaire; the speaker broached the political situation of this country. The hon. Postmaster advised economy at home, he stated that the cost of living must be reduced so as to produce cheaper, and he then proved his trust in the Conservative government.
An evidence of trust. Already the economic benefits of the numerous measures enacted have made themselves felt, not only in the return of general confidence and the resuming of work by the unemployed, but also in the growing stability of industries.
This is shown by statistics. Out of 441 companies operating public utilities or industries, 44 only have discontinued or reduced their dividends, and 397 have distributed the same dividends as in 1929, which was a record year. This, I think, is a magnificent attestation of the results attained in less than six months and due, greatly, the the energetic and farsighted policy of the government which has brought back national confidence, strengthened our industries, created work, opened markets and maintained in the path of economic stability the whole of Canada.
The speaker goes on:
To carry on the slow work of economic recovery in Canada, the government has closed the doors to all attempt of flooding the country by dumping competitive goods.
The hon. Postmaster General, sir, alluded to protection, which I look upon as exaggerated, granted to certain industries. However, is it not astonishing that the hon. Postmaster General who, it is stated, mentioned and repeated to his constituents during the elections that, if elected, he would be appointed minister of agriculture, yet, he has chosen to be Postmaster General?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
I rise to a
point of order. I wish to be indulgent for my neighbour from Terrebonne, but I must declare that I never made the statement which he attributes to me, I have better breeding than that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
In answer to the hon. Postmaster General, may' I say that I pointed out in my speech that this had been reported.
It is amazing how soon the hon. Postmaster General forgot the farmers, and allowed the Canadian market to be flooded with 2,000,000 pounds of Australian butter in the course of the last five months, When he so strongly criticized, during the election, that policy which permitted butter imports from New Zealand.
The quantities of butter imported, sir, within the last five months were out of proportion with the requirements of our population, and the government, to a degree, is responsible if, to-day, the farmers sell their butter at half-
Agricultural Conditions

price and at about the cost of production. This is a striking proof of the irrational and inconsistent policy of the Conservatives in their campaign of disparagement of the Liberal administration, when butter brought the farmers almost double of what they are receiving to-day.
Any one, sir, who glances over the speech of the hon. Postmaster General, will note that no mention is made of any measure which might give the farmers'of Quebec or those of other parts of Canada some hope. No, there is no mention of such a measure in his whole speech.
I wonder what the farmers of Laval-Two Mountains and of Quebec will think of the statement made by a member of the Bennett cabinet, that everything done heretofore by the government to inspire national confidence, has been done for the benefit of companies which pay record dividends to their shareholders, when, on the other hand, the farmers must sell all their products at wretched prices, ever since the last elections, and have no share in those record dividends. I lay stress on the word "record."
Indeed, the work of economic recovery will be very slow in the agricultural sphere as I have just pointed out to the house, and these conditions will exist as long as the government shows indifference and is neglectful of the interests of the farming community. The cost of living is reduced at the expense of the farmers. The speech from which I have just quoted extracts, as well as present conditions go to prove my contentions.
These good Conservatives, now in office, do quite the contrary to what they promised before the elections. Let us see what the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) stated on June 13, at Calgary, as reported in the Calgary Herald:
In my opinion the basic industry is agriculture. Agriculture has been the basis of this country's prosperity.
At Ormstown, on June 30, as reported by the Morning Citizen of Ottawa, Mr. Bennett, among other things, stated:
Agriculture stood first in Canadian development. We must supply the same advantages to agriculture as to other activities.
"We conservatives are pledged to see that agriculture receives the same benefits as in days gone by." Distribution and marketing were essential factors in assisting agriculture.
These statements are clear and very explicit. Yet, had the present government an end in view when they allowed, last March, 800,000 pounds of foreign butter to enter the country, which resulted in upsetting the market?
If the right hon. Prime Minister was in earnest-and I wish to give him the credit

for being so-in stating that agriculture is the basic industry of the country, that it has always been the foundation of Canada's prosperity, that it should be fostered and given the same advantages as other industries and that he pledged himself to develop this industry, why then does the government enact a high tariff-an exaggerated protection -by which only the large overcapitalized companies profit, allowing them to pay record dividends to their shareholders, as was stated by his colleague the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve)? Why did not this minister use his influence with his other colleagues in order that the farmers, who are in majority in his county, be given by the government the consideration to which they are entitled, * and thereby also draw, indirectly, dividends or profits from the sale of their products?
Another pledge was made to the electorate, previous to the elections, by the right hon. Prime Minister, on June 9, at Winnipeg, as reported by the Montreal Star:
We pledge ourselves to foster and develop agriculture, and the live stock and dairy industries, now so sadly neglected.
I draw your attention, sir, to the words "so neglected" and I think I have established by facts and authentic statements, what irony is shown by the words "so neglected" in speaking of agriculture under the Liberal regime. It behooves the farmers of Canada to think and judge whether it is not the Conservatives who, to-day, must be charged with negligence towards the farming community. The facts are there as evidence. Moreover, the action of the right hon. Prime Minister, when he refused to wait more than two minutes for the delegates of the farming classes, who came here to submit their grievances and claims before the tariff board, show pretty well his indifference towards the farming community.
There is another statement of the right hon. Prime Minister which also deserves to be pointed out to the Canadian people, and that is the one he made on June 17, at Saskatoon, as reported in the Star Phoenix. I shall give the text itself, and shall close my remarks by reverting to English as the quotations which I have yet to make are couched in that language.
There is only one way we can get the moneys of England for Canadian wheat rather than Russia and the Argentine, and how is that?
I would direct the attention of the house to the concluding words:
By providing our wheat cheaper than the others.
One can see in the inertness of the present government a possible reason; by not enacting any measures to help agriculture. Another

Agricultural Conditions
reason may be seen in the exaggerated policies of high protective tariffs where help is being given only to manufacturers and super-capitalized companies. No appropriation, either directly or indirectly, has been made out of the 120,000,000 voted for unemployment relief to help the western grain growers and the farmers of the country as a whole. The hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Sauve) has declared that in order to create faith this government has enacted measures to help industries to pay record dividends. However, he made no mention of a declaration of policy which would benefit the farmers. This is borne out by the declaration made by the right hon. Prime Minister at Saskatoon on June 19.
The agriculturists of Canada cannot but believe that the policy of this government is to drive the price of agricultural products to the bottom of the well which action would be prejudicial to the welfare of the country as a whole. The government's policy seems to be to reduce the cost of food products. This casts a burden upon the agriculturists while the manufacturers are being benefited by high protection.
These are the conditions faced by the Canadian people, and the agriculturists as a group
Farm products
are rising to condemn this government. The farmers of this country are still somewhat tickled at the report which appeared in the newspapers some time ago as to how valuable was the time of the Prime Minister. It was claimed that he did not have the necessary assistance with which to carry on his duties and had only two minutes of time to give to the farmer representatives who appeared before the tariff commissioner.
Another declaration or promise was made by the right hon. the Prime Minister at Winnipeg on June 9, as follows;
Listen, you agriculturists from the west and all the other parts of Canada, you say tariffs are only for the manufacturers. I will make them fight for you as well. I will use them to blast a way into the markets that have been closed to you.
This house and the Canadian people are interested in knowing how a way has been blasted into new markets to permit the sale of farm products. How has this been accomplished since the new administration came into office?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
In rising to address the house upon the question now before it, I am sorry indeed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is not in his seat. Allow me, however, to read the words of the amendment; which is as follows:
That all the words after the word "that" to the end of the question be left out and the following words be inserted instead thereof:
Agricultural Conditions

1.	The house regrets that the administration has failed to implement its definite promises with respect to agriculture and to this moment it has failed to announce any agriculture policy to this house.
2.	That the policies of the present administration operate to restrict, rather than to expand Canadian trade.
3.	That without the development of international trade Canadian agriculture will become increasingly paralyzed.
And further, in the opinion of the house, any policy with respect to agriculture should include emergency measures to meet the present agricultural crisis and adequate provision for the processing of meats and the marketing of live stock, wheat, dairy and of all other agricultural products.
What are the government's definite promises to Canadian agriculture? These are the Prime Minister's own words:
I shall regard it as my great responsibility, if elected on July 28, 1930, to see that the collective weight and power of the Dominion of Canada is placed behind agriculture. I would be lacking in qualifications entitling me to head a Canadian government if I failed to do so.
That is his pledge to Canadian agriculture. What have the Prime Minister and his government done to implement that pledge? I am not going to repeat the words that I uttered to the house on March 17 last, but I would like the house and the country to read those remarks in unison with what I am about to say. I then showed how, after the Imperial economic conference, the Prime Minister became wildy uproarious and left Britain with a veiled threat of economic separatism because a British minister, Mr. Thomas, mildly designated his whole proceeding as "humbug." In that respect I would like to place on Hansard this extract from the British Morning .Express:
Mr. Bennett must be very simply constituted-
I do not think this means that the right hon. gentleman is simple minded.
says the News Chronicle, if he imagines that any intelligent Englishman would be deluded by the proposal that we should tax our food m return for Canada's generosity in putting another brick on her tariff wall against foreign imports and keeping the wall at the same effective height against British goods. If that proposal is not humbug, what is it?	The
Dominion premiers like to claim the right to speak plainly and like to exercise it. They should be able to keep a stiff upper lip when an itngush statesman for once in a way speaks plainly too.
What kind of stiff upper lip did my right hon. friend keep? I am sorry he has become so touchy that hearing the simple truth should cause him to make such an exhibition of
[Mr. McMillan.!
himself as has become notorious throughout the world. To think, after receiving a degree from a great university, he should humiliate Canada by asserting that the old ties of blood and kinship between the motherland and the Dominion were gone, and that if they were not replaced by "commercial ties" -the mercenary and monetary spirit

which caused Great Britain to lose the greatest possession she has ever lost, our far-flung empire would share the fate of other great empires of the pastl WTas it not time he wa3 leaving England and the heart of our great empire, after laying down a platform such as that, and giving the quotation from the volume of the old sacred law? We could give him many quotations to show that it is the money and mercenary spirit which has caused the downfall of every great nation of the past. What was said of old Babylon? We know that in the matter of riches, in the matter of sordid wealth and outer splendour, old Babylon had no rivals in ancient times, but her fatal weakness was that she placed no weight on real manhood and -true character. As a consequence, her gorgeous palaces and hanging gardens became the abode of selfishness and sensuality with the result that we now read that over that spurious greatness rests the stillness of the desert, the gloom of an eternal night. Let him trace the downfall of every nation of the past, and he will find that that has been the cause of its fall. Is it any wonder, too, that he was not received with any great spirit of acclaim when he landed on the shores of Canada? But he hastened at once to Regina, either to prolong the hopes or to dispel the fears of the farmers of western Canada, I do not know which. To my mind it is most amusing to study the peculiar mentality of the Prime Minister. At Regina, after talking a great deal more trash he said:
Attempts are being made and would be made to fasten upon the present government responsibility for present-day conditions. But no one can deny that the present depression was only the culmination of nine years of total disregard of the fundamental principles of constitutional government, and disregard for the elementary laws of economies.
I deny that statement in toto. It is absolutely beside the fact, and if the Prime Minister knows anything, he knows that expression is some of the most arrogant piffle ever uttered by the tongue of man.
When he went to Calgary, he had rather changed his mind; he had become more hesitant, and he said he was going to find out

Agricultural Conditions
why the people of western Canada had not even the bare necessities of life. These are his words:
I cannot make up my mind why this country between the lakes and the mountains should endure such depression.
The Prime Minister seems to regard the situation in western Canada as a mere matter of psychology. He said:
Our closeness to other people has much to do with our ideas of depression. We get the idea that the whole world is out of joint, and the psychology of it is reflected in the morose and solemn way in which some men walk down the. streets of Calgary.
I tell the right hon. the Prime Minister that there is no -class of people in this world who show a finer spirit in the face of adversity than the people of western Canada, -but when men cannot sell their labour or the product of their labour, the cause and remedy must be sought in stern realities, and sir, it is stern reality which this government is giving in the villainous legislation which it has already passed, and which is grinding out the very lifeblood of the farmers of Canada. To-day all over this country the farmers are praying and pleading for a government which will relieve them of their serious fiscal burdens and increase their purchasing power by enabling them to secure access to wider and better markets in which both to buy and sell. They are praying for a government which will legislate for the general good of the people.
But let us go further. After listening to an outline of the present distressing conditions existing in many sections of western Canada, we have witnessed on two occasions in this house, on April 21 and April 28 last, the most surprising exhibition on the part of the Prime Minister. Time and again while in opposition he told the house and the country that he would prescribe for the ills of Canada once he was called in. After listening to his appeals, what is the remedy he now proposes? Mr. Speaker, it is the most humiliating spectacle I have ever witnessed in this house. He characterized the whole appeal on behalf of western agriculture as nothing more than the cry of stinking fish. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, those are the words of the Prime Minister of Canada; they are not mine. The Prime Minister declares that there is no evidence of acute distress at the moment, and he has thrown the farmers' pool into the waste basket.
He went to England and took John McFarland with him; had him appointed sales manager for the pools; he has broken down the whole line of sales communication which the wheat pool had taken years to establish, has had their sales force in Great Britain and on the continent withdrawn; has thrown the whole business back into the old channels of the grain trade, the life-long enemies and determined competition of the pool; and then after destroying the farmers' whole line of sales communication in that way, the Prime Minister has the audacity to try and convince this house that he is a friend of the pool, and he takes credit for Canada getting rid of more wheat during his regime at ruinously unprofitable prices.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am within the judgment of the house when I say there is no member who has read less of his speeches than I have since I have been a member.
After declaring that there was no evidence of acute distress among the farmers of western Canada, the Prime Minister went to the relief of the banks, and absolutely relieved the banks from the liability of losing a single dollar, and he -did that while his Minister of Agriculture was protesting against the manner in which the banks were treating the people of western Canada. What has his own Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) to say? He is reported as follows:
Credit is the desperate need of the Canadian farmer at the present time. The necessity of providing some means by which loans can be given to farmers was continuously brought to his attention. As an illustration of the reluctance of financial houses to advance money on farm property, he told of one man who was unable to borrow any money at all on a large and well-kept farm but had little difficulty in borrowing several thousand dollars on his race horses.
Again he said:
The attitude of the banks was providing the opportunity for the radical to argue that whenever capital had the chance, it reared its head to secure its toll.

Does the hon. gentleman not know that the 1929 New Zealand butter was only released from cold storage about two weeks ago?

speechtext: The hon. gentleman can study that out himself.

speechtext: Is it rot a fact that the hon. gentleman voted to cancel the New Zealand treaty, or the order in council extending the treaty to New Zealand? Why did he do so, if that order in council was so beneficial to the dairy industry?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
Yes, I did, and I am glad to answer that question. The late government gave notice of the cancellation of that order in council for the simple reason that when the Imperial conference met during the fall of that year, no Canadian government could have done anything at all unless that notice had been given. That was one of the stipulations contained in the agreement with Australia, and I recall that hon. gentlemen opposite went from one end of this Dominion to the other and never told a single audience that this condition existed. They wanted to keep the truth from the people.
So much for the dairy business. From this time henceforth the London market will regulate, in a general way, the price of Canadian butter and, as we have always informed the dairymen of Canada, the eight-cent tariff imposed on New Zealand butter is of no use. This is another instance of the sham remedy of high tariff; it vindicates every word we have said as to the folly and hypocrisy of high protection.
Now I come to the question of live stock. I hold in my hand an outline of what is purported to be Canada's new agricultural policy, and with the consent of the house I should like to be allowed to place that outline on Hansard.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
Very well, it does not amount to very much anyway. In this policy there is nothing new. If -we can only show to the live stock producers of Canada a. clear outlet by which they will be able to place their products in the hands of the ultimate consumers free from present serious obstructions and with some slight margin of profit to the producer, the problem will largely be solved. That fact is shown conclusively in the present and prospective supply of dairy products. Notwithstanding the howl that went abroad that there was a shortage in the supply of Canadian-made butter which would take years to satisfy, that shortage has disappeared within seven months.
In the Ontario section of the Canadian fat cattle trade, from the point where our animals

are dumped into the Toronto union stockyard market to where the finished product reaches the ultimate consumer the funnel is blocked so effectively that the feeder is at the mercy of the processing and distributing interests. So completely is this the case that the production of beef cattle is paralyzed to such a degree that the cattle feeder is disheartened and does not know which way to turn, with the result that our successful feeders of the past are almost entirely out of the game. No one knows what kind of a stone wall the producers are up against but those who have been actively engaged in the trade. There are no secrets in the business of meat production; there should be none in its processing and distribution. The whole business should Be an open book with no hold-up which will deprive the hard working producer of the fruits of his continuous, careful exertion. This is true also of the business of hog production, with the one redeeming feature that so far the packing combine does not seem to have all the abattoirs so effectively corailed. However, the unreasonable fluctuation in price is most exasperating to the producing partner in the game. This is a business which demands immediate, searching investigation and continuous control.
It may happen, and not infrequently does happen, that after all the wheat is garnered, transported, graded, milled or exported, it leaves no margin of profit to the grower. When this occurs the consequences are reflected at once in depressed business conditions. The partnership betwen agricultural prosperity and business prosperity now has been clearly established, and the safeguarding in every possible way of the interests of the producing partner ought to be the prime consideration of national policy.
Apart from general world conditions since the war, in the course of which nearly all nations, with the exception of Great Britain and Canada-under the Mackenzie King administration-have become high tariff crazy; apart also from the fact that international war debts should have been cancelled, the present agricultural depression in Canada is largely the result of inequality in the returns from urban and rural labour. Higher wages in urban industry and in transportation service have drawn labour from the farms to such a degree that the farm population in Ontario is incapable of properly cultivating the land. It is well known to every real student of agricultural conditiens that the farmer receives les3 return for his investment, energy and labour than any other department of our whole

Agricultural Conditions
national economic life, and yet I have never been any place on earth where this problem has received less real sympathy and true consideration than on the floor of this Canadian House of Commons.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext: Tell us how to run it, then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext: For once we will take a leaf out of the book of my hon. friend's revered leader; we will tell you when we are called in.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext: Tell us now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
You read my speech carefully and you will find that I am giving you the remedy right along.
In 1922 the Mackenzie King government started on the right lines, with a trade policy of gradually reducing tariff restrictions on all necessities, with reciprocal trade preferences towards all countries willing to meet Canada upon mutually favourable terms. These are the two factors which will tend towards a permanently successful agriculture and the encouragement of industry, shipping and international trade. In that way, and in that way only, can a Canadian government ever secure, broaden and develop the markets which Canadian agriculture must have in order to lift the Canadian farmer out of that slough of despond in which he is now placed. It is true that along the lines of lower tariff the government did advance very slowly, but in their efforts they had to overcome the obstruction of a world of advancing tariffs surrounding almost every nation. Nevertheless, under that policy the government made a wonderful record. Canadian agricultural production increased in value from $1,389,000,000 in 1922 to over $1,806,000,000 in 1928. The value of manufactured goods increased from $2,482,000,000 in 1922 to almost $4,000,000,000 in 1929, with an increase in the number of employees of manufacturing concerns from 474,430 in 1922 to 711,000 in 1929.
Canada's foreign trade also increased from $1,501,731,341 in 1922 to $2,654,574,166 in 1929, although owing to world conditions it fell back to $2,393,212,000 in 1930-a growth in which Canada led the world in her per capita exports of manufactured . and semimanufactured goods, . even leading Great Britain, France, Germany and the United States; a growth which no other nation of ten million people in any similar period of the world's history ever attained.	'
It is true that even such a record did not prevent the present world depression from partly reducing Canadian trade, along with that of other nations, in its train of economic
destruction. This shows that we are living in a world where no nation can live unto itself. In this respect I cannot help recalling that in this house some time ago I drew pointed attention to the fact that, while a policy of high tariffs had been discounted for an age, protectionists still chatter its shibboleths; that 1,028 of the leading expert economists from 46 states of the American union met President Hoover, on May 15, 1930, and made one of the strongest appeals in history against the high tariff of the United States. Some two years ago I also recalled how that great British economist, Sir George Paish, had declared that, "unless the United States and many other nations ceased telling their people, you must sell here but you must not sell there," the world was facing an economic cataclysm from which no country could escape.

The hon. member has
been speaking for forty minutes

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems too bad, after engaging ourselves during the last twenty-four hours in such pleasant entertainments, receptions and banquets, that we should now have to fall into line of battle and hear the clash of arms on the various questions that divide the parties in this house. I had a very pleasant experience listening to the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). I observed how gallantly and entertainingly he played the part of host at the luncheon we attended at noon. We have seen him in that delightful humour only too seldom during these last nine months, but once in a while these festivities make us realize how human we all are, and how friendly we can be with one another at such times. It was my good fortune to have on my right at that luncheon one of the Conservative members whose name I thought I did not know. Towards the close of the luncheon, however, I thought I would try him out to see where he came from; and lo and behold it was the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), my own old county in which I was born. At the same time, to my left, I saw my deskmate (Mr. Euler) and the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance), looking askance at me, no doubt wondering that I found such delight in the company of a one hundred per cent Tory from a constituency one hundred per cent Tory since confederation. However, we had, as the saying is, a whale of a time. We differed in politics, but that did not matter there. We like the Tories but we dislike their politics; we like

Agricultural Conditions

the sinner but we dislike the sin. That is the way we stand. But after all what good would the house be without some Conservatives? Indeed, I would resign to-morrow if there were none. Nevertheless, we cannot allow any sentimental feelings of this nature, or any sort of squeamishness to interfere with our duty to our constituents.
Before leaving for Ottawa I was invoked by my constituents, at two or three little gatherings I had of some of the executives- and when the word got around that these meetings were going to be held, there, would be .a hundred or more present-I was invoked, I say, to represent things here just as they exist in the west. I asked them what they expected me to do. I had never been in opposition before, and if we wanted to help the country it was obvious that we should have to do it through this outfit-there was no other way. I do not say that at all disparagingly, and perhaps I should not use that expression. But I think my hon. friends know what I mean. Well, at one meeting they told me what they expected of me; they said, "Tell them exactly what conditions are like in the west, because we in the prairies do not believe that they understand the situation down there." That was at one meeting. And, they added, "having performed that duty, and seeing no results, then give them hell." Now I have not carried out that invocation yet, and I do not want to go back home until I have done so, at least to some extent.
A week ago to-day, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister undoubtedly gave us on this side something of a castigation. And he can do it too. Some people call it scolding, but I call it a general tongue-thrashing. I have heard fishwives in the old country who could do it better, but I have never known any man in this country who could do it so thoroughly as the Prime Minister. I have not been brought up, either at school or anywhere else, to submit to that kind of bullying and I do not propose to start now. So that I shall have some things to say before I sit down.
Now, Mr. Speaker, ever since time was, everyone who has tried to better conditions as he has found them has been accused of discrediting his country. You may go back to old testament - history; you may turn to the various revolutions that have taken place, in the United States, in France, or in any other part of the world; you may study, more recently, the reciprocity question, and more recently still the Dunning budget, and in. every instance you will find that there have been people who have been prepaired to stand

up and say that those who have advocated improvements were endeavouring to discredit their country. And because hon. gentlemen behind me and on either side of me have been stating what they know to be the facts in western Canada, all sorts of epithets have been applied to them. But what did the Prime Minister himself say, before this parliament met, with respect to conditions in western Canada? He has been quoted on several occasions. He stated at one time, in very contrite terms, that he feared the spring would find us with no seed for the sower and no bread for the hungry. Well, that is sad enough. With the chastening influence of Christmastide upon him, and at Calgary, he did not understand how that vast country from the lakes to the mountains could not enable the farmers to lay by some reserve for an occasion like this, notwithstanding that at that time many of them were unable to secure the bare necessities of life. Could you hear anything more pessimistic than that? I have not heard anything worse. Is it wrong to say such things if they are true? Is it pessimism? Is it "stinking fish," to use the Prime Minister's expression when he spoke the other day? And what did his colleague, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), have to say? And here I wish to compliment the hon. gentleman. Sir John Macdonald used to say that the best apple tree would always be found to be the tree with the most sticks and stones under it. If that is so, my hon. friend must be the best apple tree in the orchard opposite. But what about the rest, if he is the best? I am not blaming any of them, Mr. Speaker. They have all been on the leash and under the gag of their leader. Well, that is a matter of discipline among themselves. I know what it is to be a member of the government and I sympathize with my hon. friend, because in my estimation he is not being done full justice by his leader. At Toronto I heard a friend say that the Minister of Agriculture at the Royal Winter Fair had conducted himself really creditably, and I believe he can do so in this house when he gets the opportunity. But what did the hon. gentleman say? It has been referred to by previous speakers, and I have here a quotation of some remarks of his with reference to the banks. It is about the only kudos he obtained among his various manifestos. If the rest of us require disciplining by the Prime Minister because of references we have made to the banks, what about the Prime Minister's colleague? The quotation to which I refer is from the Globe. I do not know what that paper is now politically;

Agricultural Conditions
it is supposed to be independent. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture, speaks about people being "in want." That is a very comprehensive word. The hon. member mentioned the unlikelihood of anything like secession manifesting itself in his constituency. That statement may be correct, although there may be a little corner or two where something might be heard about it. It is too bad if farmers in distress and extremity cannot say something of that nature to act as a safety valve for their vocabulary when they are backed up against the wall.
What about the Prime Minister when he was in Belfast? What did he say? He predicted the decline of the British Empire like all empires of the past unless there were applied some economic nostrums of his own making. Not a word was said against that, but the farmer out on the prairie who makes a statement as to what he thinks should be done to relieve conditions or as to what he is prepared to do if they are not bettered, is immediately castigated not by the Minister of Agriculture but by his leader and other hon. members of this house. I do not approve of that action, and I do not believe the farmer does. He wants a betterment of conditions; he is proud of Canada and he is proud of the west, but he wants to be given a chance. That is the reason he is talking in that way. Look at the example given by the Prime Minister while abroad. No one in western Canada has ever suggested the decline of the British Empire.
Another statement by my hon. friend (Mr. Weir) had to do with the lack of credit, which lack is felt very keenly by the farmers. He said, in effect, that the attitude of the banks was providing an opportunity for the radicals to advance the argument that whenever capitalism secured the opportunity it would rear its head to secure its toll. That sounds something like the remarks of my hon. friends in the haw corner of this side of the house.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext:
Well, on my left
hand.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext: Where is the gee corner?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
That was a good
bid for popularity by my hon. friend (Mr. Weir); it was good advertising; why should he work his head off without letting the world know about it? He continued:
If they (the banks) are not prepared to extend credit, someone else must and will.
I wonder who that someone is? My hon. friend was assuming the role of prophet.
22110-81*
Was he speaking for his sleeping colleagues? Will they not wake up from their stupor and advise us who this benefactor is? Who is this man who is going to supply credit? My hon. friend has a grand opportunity to tell us; he would sweep things before him and would have everything his own way.
If the Prime Minister intends to castigate the hon. members of this side of the house, let him turn to the Minister of Agriculture, who has been on the leash so long. I prefer not to make many comments with regard to my successor. I had a delightful experience with my predecessor and I would have liked to have handed that on. However, there are those I regard more highly even than my successor, and that is my constituents.
I have recited before the various and varied experiences of the Prime Minister during the last nine months, but I will hurriedly go over them again. What did he do to assist interempire trade on the very day he took train for Quebec to embark for London-he put up the tariff as an indication of affection and good will towards the motherland. Would not that take the beard right off anyone? Certain wild animals in captivity show their affection for their young by devouring them. Take the mother fox, for instance; if you disturb her she will eat her young or smother them because of her love. That is t'he way the Prime Minister showed his love for interempire trade-by smothering it. How strangely some people display their affection! We see in his London experience an attempt to eat Hon. Mr. Thomas without salt. There was also the Manchester Guardian incident, the cotton spinner and shoemaker incidents, and then again at Belfast where he was being honoured with a degree. He said the most extraordinary things there, such things as one would expect to come from a rattlebrain, but we do not suspect the Prime Minister of being that. I do not think that there is a hole between here and hades into which the Prime Minister has not put his foot to the hilt during these last nine months. I see by the countenances of hon gentlemen opposite that they all agree with me in this, because none knoweth better than they.
We will have a vote on this question and we will be interested in seeing how our western Tories will vote. Of course they will vote right, and for that reason we will have to be as pleasant as possible in putting up with Tory policies for the next three or four years.
We are being asked: what would we do? I do not think that is a fair question, but I intend to accept it as one. In the past no opposition leader or opposition that I know of
Agricultural Conditions

has ever produced a policy for the government, nor should they be expected to. People call in a new doctor and no matter how much of a fake that doctor may he it is a violation of medical practice and etiquette for the old doctor to nose in unless he is urgently asked to do so. We have been so repeatedly and almost urgently asked to supply a policy, that I think I will do so, with limitations. Many hon. members will recall that in the fall of 1929 the Department of Agriculture through its officers-for a time assisted by myself just before I went to the hospital in December-realized that things were sliding with regard to the live stock industry. Wheat had been such an attractive proposition in the west in previous years that the production of live stock in some lines had been permitted to decrease in relation to consumption. It had not kept up with the consumption in Canada because of the extraordinary developments during the previous five or six years. We had the home market which our Tory friends love so well and we were just able to keep up with the consuming and purchasing capacity of the people during the growing and *developing years from 1923 to 1929. However, I did not like to see our exports disappearing off the British market, and my then deputy and my then self took an initial step and got out some 1,200 questionnaires with the view of increasing the production of live stock in Canada. Certain agricultural papers strongly opposed a greater production program, even in this province-some in the city of Toronto-and in order to be fair to the others I might mention the Canadian Countryman. However, these papers had a right to express their thoughts on this matter. Out of the 1,200 questionnaires which were returned, mostly -from farmers, we found that two-fifths were either against this suggested increased production or indifferent to it, while three-fifths vere fairly strong for it, particularly if the government would provide some additional means of marketing the increased production. It was suggested that a number of experimental abattoirs should be established, along similar lines to the experimental creameries at Finch, which would demonstrate the value of lessening costs by mass production. A live stock conference was held in my then office in March, 1930, but there were too many present to permit the formulation of any definite policy. There were forty in attendance, every one with views and opinions of his own, but we had received sufficient information as to the feelings of the farmers and their live stock organization to realize that some forward step should and could be rMr. Motherwell.]
taken with fair prospects of public sentiment among farmers being behind it. This will be found recorded in Hansard of last year, although not quite so fully as now.
In the meantime I had recovered sufficiently to get on my pins, although not much more. We had to "give some effect to that sentiment, assuming of course we were going to come back to power, although on that score I had a few misgivings of my own. Possibly my being ill accounted for them. As a matter of fact, however, if hon. gentlemen care to hunt up the supplementary estimates of last spring they will find that, on my advice to my colleagues, there was placed in the supplementary estimates an item of $25,000 for a thorough investigation into the live stock industry, including live stock products and all things associated with live stock, that is seeding down, drifting soil, and many things that require to be gone into thoroughly before one embarks on a big campaign of increased live stock production, especially in western Canada.
Of course we know what intervened. The electors thought our hon. friends opposite could do better. They have been quite disabused of that idea by now, but my hon. friends opposite are in power and what can we do but make suggestions? If they call for the files, they will find it is on record that the money was there for a live stock inquiry, and the present government did not choose to use it. They apparently thought they could evolve a better plan without anybody outside of themselves telling them what to do, with only one gentleman in the cabinet being a recognized authority, and he with a limited experience as to years-three years' residential experience on the farm. He (Mr. Weir) was the only agricultural authority within the cabinet, and a great responsibility surely rested upon his shoulders. They also seemed to spurn the idea of seeking outside advice, possibly because of the known objection to commissions generally entertained by more or less uninformed individuals. Nevertheless they had a commission, the Stamp commission, composed of eminent gentlemen. I could never find out who asked the government for it. It is not safe to predict before the event, but I will take my chances on predicting that the result will be just about what we all knew before, namely, that you cannot dispense with future marketing, future selling; but that certain limitations will be put upon it. It will be something like what is in practice in Chicago and Kansas City. This shows that it was not hostility to commissions that led the government to take

Agricultural Conditions
the course they did, but simply that they thought they were all sufficient in themselves to formulate a policy regarding live stock and live stock products.
My good friend is desiirous of proving himself fully qualified to fill the very difficult position he now occupies. He has my sympathy, and I am not going to recite all the policies that he has evolved, and that, have been increasing in numbers as the months go by. In the beginning he had only four items, and they looked a little small to be called a new national policy. He was going to take care of pollorum in chickens, something that has been rampant in some flocks in Canada for fifteen years. This is not something new. Ask the chickens in the maritimes if it is new. They were so affected. Ask the Dominion poultrvman. Why, if there is one branch of agriculture that has been developed in the last five, six or eight years in Canada, it has been poultry, and the diseases are the constant attention of the departmental officials. Yet my modest friend is going to cure pollorum, which is "white scour" in chickens. This is a commendable and very necessary work, but surely it cannot be called new any more than the agriculture of King Tut can be called new. Wheat has been found in those catacombs or bowels of the earth, whatever you call them, and this indicates that there was an agriculture in those days. What is field agriculture? It is the developing and growing of selected domestic plants good to nourish man and beast. Consequently there was nothing new about that.
Some months later in MacLean's, a very enterprising magazine, a Mr. Churchill had an interview with my hon. friend. In a moment of weakness he unfolded himself further with regard to policies. He has evidently a good standing with the press and he has given them a good story. Anyone who gives the press a good story will receive a good hearing from them, but sometimes it is inconvenient to talk as freely as one might and especially when the very self-same policy, which was unfolded in MacLean's magazine, was unfolded in that good old farmers' journal, the Farmers' Advocate, on which I was brought up. Nevertheless to make it more official, we find it in the library of the Department of Agriculture: "Descriptive List of Accessions." This is supposed to cover the books. This is not a book: this is an accession which I am going to read:
Canada's new agricultural policy; an exclusive and authentic statement of the new farm policy shortly to be announced in parliament by the Hon. Robert Weir, Minister of Agriculture. by R. Churchill (in MaeLean's magazine, March 15, 1931, pages 12, 64).
Canada's new agricultural policy consists of-
-so and so. We have to take that as official. I think my hon. friend will nol object to my taking it as official. It may have got in there without his knowledge, because in my experience I have found the most extraordinary things happen without a man's knowledge; but not knowing anything different, until recently we have had to take this as only semi-official, particularly when associated with the Prime Minister's remarks the other day when some of our more pertinent members from Saskatchewan, shall I say, wanted to know more about this matter. He the Prime Minister said that the Minister of Agriculture was a practical farmer-I almost heard the smile that came over their faces at that- intimation-and that he had very decided views on certain phases of agriculture, which views would be divulged when his estimates were before the house. Consquently this magazine policy is not the official announcement after all, and so far as I can see we are just wasting our time on it. The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and the hon. member for Southeast. Grey (Miss Macphail) went over it so effectively that in charity I shall not deal with it any further. As my time is going on, I shall simply proceed with my further remarks.
What do I propose? I have a hunch that none of these manifestoes or policies is the real Kildare. There is another one coming. I say so for the simple reason that none of them was worth a snap of the fingers. As the kindergarten of agriculture, they were all 100 per cent genuine; they were largely elementary-, rudimentary and good in their place, but they were not what the farmers on the prairies or down here are thinking about just now. If anyone were to go into a farmers' meeting such as was held in Saskatoon this last winter with that so called new government policy, 1 would not guarantee his getting out without some bodily injury. That is the case, and the hon. member knows it. But I want to commend the Minister of Agriculture for trying to do his best without the assistance of any in the cabinet with any experience except that they were born on the farm or as they went to school saw, through the cracks in the fence, somebody farming.
That anticipated live stock commission which never materialized expected to look into a number of phases of the question. I had not any cut and dried proposition, but if I had to bring the matter up myself, I had in mind something forward to do with the development of the dairy industry. Our opponents, rivals, competitors, all over the world for the last twenty-five years have been gradually developing and enlarging the manu-
Agricultural Conditions

factoring units of their dairy products and increasing the production of the production unit, the cow, increasing the flow of her milk and increasing the size of the dairy buildings until they are eight or ten times as large as they were fifty or sixty years ago when dairy and cheese factories were started in Ontario. That has been going on for twenty-five years in both the United States and New Zealand. Our present dairy commissioner was the chief resident factor and adviser in starting up the present dairy industry in New Zealand. Doctor Ruddick knows all about these plants, and of what advantage it is to have a large production in each one, which tends not only to quality and cheapness of production but to uniformity of product, which is so acceptable on the markets of any country. In our own country, through the effluxion of time, the old junk factories, which were all right at the beginning, are disappearing, and better ones are taking their place; but if we leave it to the process of evolution I am afraid it will take us about a hundred years before we can compete successfully in dairy products with our competitors throughout the world. We can compete now, yes, but it is a competition that leaves our dairyman skinned right down to the heels; there is nothing left for him at all, with cheese at nine cents and butter at twenty and twenty-two cents a pound. They need government help; and let the government take action now. The thought I have in mind now is what I had in mind when I was minister and when S25,000 was put in the estimates of 1930 for a live stock inquiry; and it looks even better now than it did then, because this government is committed as no previous government ever was to putting the whole weight and power of this Dominion behind agriculture, as was promised at the last election. My good friend the Minister of Agriculture can ask for almost anything from this government for agriculture, and if he secures it I can assure him that he will have a solid phalanx of this side of the house behind him too. It is said that we sometimes play politics, but in view of the present distressing conditions in the west, the member of parliament who plays politics alone will not last very long. They want us to be big enough to stand up and help the government in anything that will be of benefit to agriculture, even though we oppose the general policies of the government. I see the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Loucks) nodding his head. I hope he will nod it in an effective manner when this question comes to a vote. He knows agriculture, and so does my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. 
Perley). They are both extensive practical farmers in the west.
That is the thought I had in mind; and not only that, but its companion industry, the meat packing business. Whether rightly or wrongly, the producers of live stock in Canada have no confidence in the abattoirs. I do not think that feeling is quite justified, although to some extent it may be. I do not think the abattoirs have been making a nickel in the last few years because of a lack of supply of the raw material; the farmers are not supplying it because they have no confidence in the packers. The thing continues in a vicious circle, neither the farmers nor the packers, as to supply of raw material, having confidence in the other. We have had an increased activity in recent years on the part of the Canadian Live Stock Cooperative Association Limited, and that body hopes for a friendly abattoir in which to process their live animals. What was in our minds at the time we had the conference in my office when I was minister was that we would have an experimental packing plant so that we could ascertain the cost of processing, and find out just what was the reason for the ghastly spread between the cost of the live hog and the finished meat. We thought of one experimental plant in the east and one in the west as a starter. Everybody who has been to Europe, especially Denmark, knows that dairying alone would fall down, and hog raising alone would fall down; but the two together make a go of it, because one is the complement of the other. So I say that it is high time we got a start along the line of properly constructed and standardized combination creameries and butter factories, capable of handling milk and converting it into the most profitable product at the particular time of production. Other nations are doing that already, and we must do it if dairying is going to continue in this country and we are to meet changed conditions abroad. It was with that idea in mind that this prospective commission was thought of, which never was born; nevertheless it may yet come to life. I hope it will, because it is not in the boots of any one man in this Dominion to lay out a proper policy for advanced present-day agriculture by himself. We want the combined knowledge and experience of the very best three or five men that we can find in this Dominion, or, if necessary, we should go beyond the Dominion; but I do not think that is necessary.
Let me ask the Minister of Agriculture not to be shy in following in the footsteps that I endeavoured to trace out for him in this re-

Agricultural Conditions
spect. I know how hard it is to do that, but perhaps he will be able to do something along the same line-anything, so long as we get proper and effective action. When the Prime Minister was over in London at the Imperial conference, how often we heard the excuse made on his behalf, "Well, at any rate, we are getting action." That is what the fellow said when he was going over Niagara falls in a barrel; but where was the action taking him to?
I shall not dwell much longer on the dairy industry. It is not my business to evolve government policies, but they helplessly call for it. For the sum of $50,000 a standardized creamery can be established. We have one in Finch, Ontario. It was established in the time of the Hon. Martin Burrell, just to demonstrate this one point I have been making. I do not claim that my proposal is new, but I say it is high time that the idea was given a trial, especially with butter and eggs selling at just a little better than half what they were selling at one year ago. Something must be done, and if anybody has any better idea I will at once dismiss mine and fall in behind that better one, but I want to be shown the better one first. The receipts of the plant at Finch increased from
2,000,000 pounds in 1912 to 11,000,000 pounds in 1925; that poundage includes the various products into which the milk and cream was made. The operations of that plant resulted in an increase from. 10 to 31 cents per hundred which the plant was able to pay to its patrons for their milk. There was such a rush of dairymen to get milk sale accommodation in that factory that we were really embarrassed. Having got all the information we wanted from our operation of that Finch plant, we sold it for $25,000, which was the initial cost to the government. So the experiment meant no loss at all to the government, and it was of tremendous benefit to those particular farmers, and of tremendous benefit also to all those who followed the Hon. Martin Burrell in completing the superstructure on the foundation which he had laid. I think the department had something to do with it too. Doctor Ruddick knew the effective competition of New Zealand with larger dual factories, but we have to give the minister in charge the full credit which is coming to him because, after all, he had to dig up the coin for it, and that is no easy matter sometimes.
This dairy policy which I am suggesting, and which has been forced upon us by conditions in competitive countries, has already been started at Finch, and when we find the government so teetotally pledged to the hilt
to get behind agriculture in this country, is it not time they were moving? Are we going to be met with the old stereotyped excuse that was given to us the other day in regard to needed public buildings, that it is hard to get the money? It is always hard to get money, and admittedly sometimes it is harder than others, but if this government puts up its tariff wall so high as to exclude imports, what can it expect but diminished revenues? If the government cannot get money anywhere else, what about the claim of the hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) against the Department of Trade and Commerce in connection with the handling of the 1917-18 crop? I would like to see a little more about that. Probably the western farmers might lend the interest on that money, which would amount to about $20,000,000, to prime the pump, as it were, and start the thing going. Anything to get action, but not in the direction I was speaking of a minute ago. We have these two factors:	The government is pledged to get
behind agriculture, and there is this second factor that nc industry is so closely associated with the health of the nation and the fertility of the soil as the dairying industry, and therefore I believe that the government would be justified in going to almost any limit in reason towards that desired end. They could start with an item in the estimates of $1,000,000, with the two old provinces of Quebec and Ontario each contributing $500,-
000.	That would make a total of $2,000,000, with which you could construct forty up-to-date standardized combined-cheese, butter, etc.-dairy plants at a cost of $50,000 per plant. In ten years you would have four hundred. That seems to me reasonable. You cannot do it all at once. These parliament buildings were not all put up at once. The central buildings were erected first, then the east block, then the west block, later on the Connaught building, recently the Confederation block, and there will be other buildings later on. Only let us make a start in this matter. I suggest to my hon. friend that he start-but not in the direction of Niagara falls.
There is the example at Finch. It is not a model creamery, because the original building was added to from time to time until it became a combination of rookeries. Still it did better than a small creamery. Attempts in this direction have been made in the province of Quebec, but, oh, the established institutions, dating back fifty or sixty years, are hard to root up, so sacred do such local rural associations become. Private interests have their money invested in those little cheese
Agricultural Conditions

factories turning out three or four cheeses a day. How can they make them pay on that small production? How can they afford to engage a proper cheesemaker?-and yet they make wonderful fine cheese therein. It may be that those private interests will have to be indemnified. The cost is so great if undertaken alone by the provinces, and the necessity is so urgent that I appeal to my hon. friends to say if this is not a good time to undertake cooperation action with the provinces. It is not new. I am prepared to hand the credit back to the Hon. Martin Burrell, to anybody, as long as we get something done.
Then we have our grain marketing. Unless there is a mighty quick right-about we are riding for a fall again there at the coming London conference. I do not think my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Weir) knows anything about grain marketing. He is a live stock man, a prize-winner, but I do not think he claims to be an authority on the marketing of grain any more than I am. There used to be one man in this house, the Hon. C. A. Dunning, whom I looked upon as the greatest authority in Canadian public life on grain marketing. Well, we will have to try to get along without him at present. But we have had a grain conference at Rome. Mr. Ferguson I notice, has got into trouble there with the Orange order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the representative of a riding almost entirely agricultural, I take great pleasure in supporting the motion offered by the hon member from Lisgar (Mr. Brown). It is readily seen that the agricultural class has not been receiving all the consideration it was entitled to expect from those elected to power last July. The pledges made during the campaign had led us to believe that agriculture was to be revolutionized. Our farmers were almost sure that their produce was going to bring extraordinarily high prices. But what did happen? If the hon. member for Lisgar brings down a motion of non-confidence, on the agricultural issue, I feel' certain that the least surprised of all are the members of the Conservative party; what surprises them most is that this motion was not brought up before. What have we witnessed since these gentlemen came into power? First of all, at the emergency session of last September, when we voted
820,000,000 for the relief of unemployment throughout Canada, rather extraordinary powers were given the minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryckman), and a large number of items in our customs tariff were revised. Certain short items, here and there, in the newspapers sought to convey the impression that promises made to farmers were being implemented, for instance through the tariff increase on butter, and like products. But today we can clearly see that these changes brought no relief to the farming community as they were led to expect from the pledges made during the last campaign. At this advanced stage of the session it is high time that the hon. minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) should define the government's policy on the matter of agriculture. From both sides of the house it has been stated that the agricultural crisis is the worst in Canada at the present time. Nevertheless when certain activities of the department were under discussion and the minister asked if that were his policy, whether the four sections of his program were quoted or whether the said program were published in MacLean's magazine, I believe his answer always was that these were merely some of the activities of his department, and that they were not his entire program. After all the promises made by the Conservative party I think the Canadian farmer was entitled to expect at the

Agricultural Conditions
very least a definite program for the protection of agriculture, and that quite some time ago.
On this score I wish to quote from a speech made at Winnipeg by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) during the course of the campaign. Amongst other things he said the following:
Listen, you agriculturists from the west and all the other parts of Canada, you have been taught to look down upon the customs tariff and to pin your faith to free trade. Tell me, when did free trade ever benefit you? You say tariffs are only for the manufacturers. I will make them fight for you as well. I will use them to blast a way into the markets that have been closed to you.
Mr. Speaker, after statements like that were made repeatedly throughout the country. is it any wonder that our farmers began to believe they were at the dawn of a new day? They were told that the Canadian market had been flooded with New Zealand butter, that the Canadian farmer was not reaping enough profit on his produce, in consideration of the labour their production entailed, their situation was shown in a very bad light. They agreed that there was some truth in this and felt that the Conservative party really did intend to help them through a policy quite different from that actually put into practice.
Let us see what has happened since the Conservative party came into power and since they raised the tariff on butter. No new duty was levied on cheese because it was recognized that the price of this product was necessarily fixed by conditions on the world market. But the very fact that the duties on cheese were not raised-cheese being one of the most important of our dairy products-goes to show, does it not, that a tariff is of no use to the dairy industry since its production can bring only the price set by the markets of the entire world.
To-day the farmer is much worse off than before. An analysis of the present situation -these figures have been quoted on several occasions on the floor of the house, but I intend repeating them because I wish to draw them to the particular attention of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir)-shows that the price of butter has dropped considerably on the Montreal market within the last few days. After this weakening movement, the hon. Minister of Agriculture had a conference with Mr. T. W. Grieve, Mr. A. Me-Kergow, Mr. K. D. Olive and Mr. John Charest, all butter merchants in Montreal. Since the conference we have heard it said that certain suggestions had been made by
the hon. Minister of Agriculture-for instance, that butter be stored until later. I do not know whether I should attribute this advice to the hon. minister because I should have to ask him if he thought the suggestion very wise. I do not wish to be too severe towards the hon. Minister of Agriculture, who is himself a farmer, and has had the fact broadcast from one end of Canada to the other by the Conservative party; still we would like to see him rise to the situation and really do something for agriculture. Under the circumstances I believe I am well within my rights in putting him this question: What was the result of your meeting with the butter importers and merchants in Montreal? We certainly would like to know; and the farmers of the entire country ask you this question which appears to me to be fair, reasonable and timely just now.
The right hon. Prime Minister promised (he farmer that all his ills would be remedied by the tariff ; and we had the right to expect that the leader of the government would adopt a policy favourable to the farming community. Once more I say to the hon. Minister of Agriculture that the session is already well along and that still no policy has been announced. We trust that before the present debate is ended he will deem it his duty to reveal just what his program is in relation to Canadian agriculture. A visit to our different country markets during the last few weeks proves that the real situation is very far from that all these promises led us to expect.
During the campaign we were given to understand that the increase in customs duties would enhance the prices of agricultural produce and that the farmer would be protected like the other classes of the community.
According to the statistics disclosed on the floor of this house-these figures are known to all our Canadian citizens, because to-day the situation is being studied more than ever before-there is no reduction, or very little, in the price of the necessaries of life, while the prices of agricultural produce are constantly on the down-grade; as a consequence the condition of this industry in our Dominion is very bad, not to say desperate. But to come back to what we noticed: The difference in prices on the markets is so great that housewives are always surprised when they compare this years' prices with those they had to pay last year. But those who are most surprised and who feel it most are the farmers who see the prices of their products striking bottom all along the line. Here are a few facts revealed by an investigation made last
Agricultural Conditions

we may say that the farmer, although very often he is not so well-equipped as he would wish to be, and sometimes has not the money necessary for improvements, spent last $1.05 per 100 pounds of milk. And although there has been a decrease in the price of grain no one can show that the farmer is in a position to care for his herd throughout the year, to pay the wages of his help, and to sell milk at 65 or 70 cents per 100 pounds. It is plain therefore that the farmer is working at a loss. If the dairy industry is the main industry of a majority in the province of Ontario, and of quite a number of farming districts in the province of Quebec, how can the farmers get along if they continue to receive such low prices?
During the last campaign the farmers were given to understand that the tariff would come to their assistance, that new markets would be opened up for their products and that they w.ould sell their produce at reasonable prices. If the conservative candidates at that time found that the farmers were not receiving reasonable prices, I ask them if to-day, after eight months of conservative administration, they consider prices reasonable: butter, 22 cents a pound; cheese, 9 cents; eggs 15 to 17 cents a dozen, and so forth. Prices have fallen outrageously since the conservative party came into power.
Quite everybody agrees to-day that the agricultural class carries the largest share of the burden of taxation, be it the customs tariff, the sales tax, or whatever else; that is to say that the farmers are taxed not only on property they own, but further on values which they do not possess. While I do not wish to make any comparison with other provinces, let me tell you that we, in the province of Ontario, where we are ruled over by a conservative government,-a past-master, believe me, at the art of tax-raising: I am really convinced that no other province in the world derives as much revenue from natural resources - of whatever kind-still our government never succeed in meeting expenses, despite all the taxes they impose; they always end up with a deficit.
