speechtext: Take Quebec.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
speechtext:
I intend mentioning later some of the taxes that must be paid. Very often the government sidesteps the responsibility of collecting the tax directly and acts through the county council. To-day our county councils are recognized as being collection agencies for the political machine at Toronto. This is so far true that the Ontario farmer must pay to the province, not directly

but through the county council, 20 per cent of the cost of construction and upkeep of provincial roads; we must pay 50 per cent of the construction of county roads, and 70 per cent of the cost of all township highways. Furthermore we must bear the entire cost of the administration of justice. This administration is in the hands of the provincial government, but the bill is sent to the county council which collects from the ratepayers and pays the bills. We must pay our share of the cost of administering the Mothers' Allowance Act, an excellent piece of social legislation, which I would be the last man to criticize. However, we bear a part of the cost of this tax, as also of the Old Age Pensions. We pay for the protection of children, for treatment given under the Hospitals Act, for primary and secondary schools, for school grants, and for the general administration of the municipalities and counties. Apart from that we must contribute towards debentures and the extinction of the local debt. The farmers bear the largest share of this burden of taxation.
Consequently it is little wonder that the farmers cannot stay on their land. The older generation try to hang on just as long as they can; but the youngsters are far less attached to the soil. What makes the oldsters try so hard to cling to their farms is that they have given 20 or 25 years of their lives to unceasing efforts in cultivating the land and striving to rid it of encumbrances. If during the last few years this older generation of farmers have succeeded in paying $2,000, $3,000 of $4,000 towards the settlement of their indebtedness; if to-day they find themselves so burdened with taxes that they cannot pay these taxes and their interest, and still earn a living, they at least do all they can to hold on to their equity, so as not to lose what they earned in years gone by.
But the new generation, not having given so much effort to the farm, are infinitely less interested. There you have one of the reasons why our young farmers are drifting into our cities and swelling the ranks of the unemployed. There is nothing surprising in the fact that from the month of September, 1930, to to-day, the number of unemployed rose from 117,000 to 300,000. The Conservatives cannot deny these figures now.

Agricultural Conditions
present prices of agricultural produce with those of last year he will be ashamed of his remark.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, all I have to say is simply this:	If the Conservatives
really believe that agriculture is the foundation of our entire economic system; if they really believe that Canadian prosperity depends on that class who produce the necessaries of life; if they believe that the prosperity of our country can only come through the prosperity of Canadian agriculture, then it is high time to make an about turn: let the prices of farm produce increase, let there be a reduction in the other necessaries of life. At the present time there is no economic balance; the situation is so utterly unequal that the farmer is getting beyond his depth, while the other classes of the community, who are protected, can still enjoy the fruits of their labour and safeguard the value of their property. Is that a proper balance? Is that prosperity? Before resuming my seat I make a special appeal to the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). I say to him that this class must obtain something; it is absolutely necessary. Since the prices of their products are determined by world markets and we cannot increase them, for we must compete against other countries, then the goods farmers need must be brought within their reach and not be protected by fictitious tariffs which only result in creating enormous wealth, for a few captains of industry, from the sweat and toil of the farmer.

speechtext:
We had
hoped that with the change of government all our farmers would be happy after eight or nine months of a new administration. They are not. People in the country complain. We were told in the course of the debate on the address in * reply to the speech from the
throne, that we spoke too much of butter, hens and eggs. We shall, sir, never speak enough, because our opponents made an abuse of it last summer. Those who accepted everything they were being told as if it were the word of the gospel, are inclined to say today: we were deceived, the market has fallen through. I ask the government whether it is possible for them to raise our people's morale and prevent market dips as took place last week, 10 cents per week is too much.
The fact remains that, to whatever class we belong, we depend on the farming classes. Whether we be lawyers, doctors, merchants or anything else, we acknowledge that the farm is the foundation of all our institutions, and when you disturb it-you may threaten it to win elections-von disturb the vital parts of our economic structure.
If you do not fulfil your pledges to them, it will be your condemnation; at present, they are suffering; but beware of the future.
Have conditions improved since last July? I simply put the question and leave it to you to answer. Our people under the spell of fine pledges, splendid speeches delivered in public, changed their allegiance, thinking perhaps, that conditions would improve. Have they improved?

speechtext:
Not so bad, but it is worse to-day. Those who changed their allegiance hoped that in doing so an improvement would take place. They now find that conditions have never been worse.
The question under consideration has been debated at length, I do not wish to scrutinize all the arguments that- have been so well discussed in the house. May I, however, submit for the consideration of the house, eertain suggestions although not new-they are inspired by excellent motives

they should nevertheless help the government in drawing up legislation which will help the 'farmers. I am aware that the government's intentions are the very 'best, I therefore do not wish to be unfair towards them. Their intentions are good, but they move too slowly. I do not mean that they are lazy, but the measures are slow in coming. I admit the government's good -intentions, however, may I ask that they expedite matters as our people -are in distress and the blame falls on the government, especially when the government contends that the depression was due to the King administration, now that they are in office what are we to expect.
Agricultural Conditions

May I, sir, make certain suggestions to the house, which are very simple and will toe readily understood, they have been prompted by the needs of the farmers of my riding. My constituents have the same needs as those of other ridings, their needs are those of the farming class.
I know that- the government recognize that there is a wound, a sore spot which they seek to heal, they have been seeking a remedy for the last nine months. Let them apply the remedy which will permit us to tell the people: The government which you have elected have found a cure. The government have no further need of seeking a panacea.
I wish to make known certain facts that I have observed in my riding and which, I trust, will serve, together with others that have been brought to the attention of the House, to solve the difficult problems which beset the government.
You are aware that, for ever so long, in fact it has never been otherwise, the farmer lives on the products of his farm, in some districts in Quebec, however, he also seeks outside the limits of his farm additional means to meet the needs of his family. He depends on his farm but to some extent on his sales of pulpwood as a side line. For the last few years, sir, the pulpwood industry has gone down and the reason given, is that our pulp mills have to compete with large foreign concerns, this obliges the merchant to put in the market a No. 1 product. Such is the situation. Our people are willing to do almost the impossible to supply the market with a product of superior quality, however, they must secure returns commensurate with their efforts. If the government are in earnest, if they really intend to help farmers, why not, while enacting measures to better the lot of large concerns for whom I have great respect and whose prosperity I wish to further, consider also the lot of those who are operating on a small scale, in the pulpwood industry. If in earnest, they will act immediately, if not, they will continue as they have done for the last nine months, that is do nothing.
In 1927, sir, the Liberal government enacted the Farm Loan measure and established in each province a board to look after the ad-Ininistration of the act and carry out its provisions. speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, May 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Woods-worth for the second reading of Bill No. 19, to amend the criminal code.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN.
subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENT
subsubtopic: NATURE OF SPEECHES ON PUBLIC AFFAIRS TO DETERMINE UNLAWFUL ASSEMBLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal the other evening I was attempting to show the conditions which exist in some of our Canadian cities which have led me to introduce this amendment. I had referred to a statement which appeared in Toronto Saturday Night which referred to the Toronto police as follows:
They have attempted to suspend the laws protecting free speech and free assembly in the case of a band of gentle idealists known as the Toronto branch of the Fellowship of Reconciliation.
Later on Toronto Saturday Night speaks of the sixty-eight professors, lecturers and instructors of the university of Toronto who declared that attempts to nullify or restrict one of the proudest heritages of the British people, that is, free speech, were shortsighted, inexpedient and intolerable; in the opinion of Saturday Night they were worse than that-they were criminal. I referred also to the representations on behalf of the Fellowship of Reconciliation which had been made by Doctor Salem G. Bland. I will quote again one sentence, as follows:
What the Fellowship of Reconciliation does protest against is that a policeman, high or low, should take the law unto himself and decide in advance whether a meeting is going to be lawful or not. What right has he to judge beforehand?
Rabbi Eisendrath said:
Nor can any rectification of the present attitude toward our own society content us unless the same liberty be guaranteed to the humblest and most helpless, the most friendless of Our fellow-citizens, however mistaken and unpopular his views may be.

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
I mentioned the interference with certain groups in Toronto during the last elections, which led Colonel 0. M. Biggar to write as follows:
If these-
Referring to certain allegations:
-are true it would appear that there has been established in Toronto what can only be properly described as a police tyranny entirely outside the law-, and that they should be true would be incredible apart from the absence of any satisfactory denial or explanation of the allegations made by Mr. Cohen in his previous communication. The real question raised by these and Mr. Cohen's present letter is the question whether in Toronto the police are enforcing the law or are persecuting persons who hold opinions of which they disapprove by the confiscation of printed matter found in their possession, by physical violence, by the misuse of licensing powers, and by threat of the institution of criminal proceedings for which there is no foundation.
The response made to this letter of Colonel Biggar's is typical of the attitude of the police. It was stated that the police were apprehensive of a serious breach of the peace and a charge of vagrancy was laid against one man. The police statement is rather curious, being as follows:
When Ewan appeared in the police court the charge was withdrawn upon his stating that he was leaving the country for Europe on the following day. I do not know whether vagrancy was the proper charge in this case, or not. Probably one of the subsections of the vagrancy section would apply, but I am quite sure the charge of obstructing a police officer in the execution of his duty, or a breach of the city by-law would have been appropriate and that in this case Ewan was most generously dealt with by being permitted to go on his assurance that he was going to Europe.
This statement by the police officers themselves would go to show that they wanted to get rid of this man; they thought him undesirable and they considered the meeting which he was addressing to be an unlawful assembly. They were willing to charge him with vagrancy, and if that charge was not good enough, they thought they could substitute for it one of obstructing a police officer.
Several years ago a conviction against Harvey Murphy was appealed. On September 12, 1929, Mr. Justice Raney quashed the conviction and ordered the police to pay the costs. In delivering judgment, Mr. Justice Raney said:
One cannot help from reading the evidence but be impressed with the view that this police court case was the outcome of an attempt to hold a meeting by people who call themselves communists. If there was any offence that was
the offence .... what disturbance was there except that created by the police? ... I have been referred to no authority which makes refusing to move when instructed by a police officer an offence under the criminal code.
There are certain ways in which the police may proceed; at times they may insist that people move on, but I submit that attention should be paid to this decision of Mr. Justice Raney, that it is not a crime under the criminal code for a man to refuse to move on when instructed.
The police of Toronto are not the only ones who have adopted a very highhanded attitude in this regard. I should like to read a few extracts from an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of April 6, as follows:
Police heads in Montreal are seeking within the ranks of their subordinates for three detectives against whom warrants have been issued charging common assault.
The article continues:
The. warrants arise out of a suspected communist meeting, and out of "communist literature" which, when dropped by the small boy who was thought to be carrying it. oozed out onto the sidewalk in yokes and whites of eggs.
And again.
For some time a group of young people, interested in current events, social movements and books, have been gathering in private homes under the name of "The Saturday Night Club." There they discussed everything under the sun, agreed and disagreed with one another, and listened to speakers expound their specialties.
And in conclusion:
The nature of the Saturday Night Club, which was suspected of communist activities, is best indicated by a partial list of speakers who have addressed it. Among them were G. H. Corbett, secretary of the Society for the Protection of Women and Children; Rabbi Stern, of the -Temple Emmanu'El; Mrs. Kensett of the Children's Bureau; H. S. Ross. K.C., Doctor Silverman, of the Mental Hygiene Clinic; C. P. Rice, and A. Heaps, M.P. for Winnipeg North.
It does seem ridiculous that the police of Montreal and the detectives who are more or less under their direction should not only undertake to supervise public halls but should actually maintain a system of espionage with regard to private homes. In this particular case a boy who was delivering eggs to the home was actually maltreated by the police, and action was taken against them. When private homes are put under surveillance like that, it seems to me it is time some further action is taken.
Not only have we this attitude on the part of the police in eastern cities, but the western police are beginning to copy their methods. I hold in my hand a copy of the
1276	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
Star-Phoenix of Saskatoon in which there is a despatch from North Battleford under date of April 13:
Claiming that there was too much talk of force, revolution and bloodshed in the offing. Chief of Police D. Felker on Saturday placed a ban on meetings of the North Battleford Open Forum in the Savoy cafe here, after a sixth meeting was addressed by Magistrate J. H. Greaves.
The article goes on:
It is understood that the ban on the Open Forum meetings applies only to the Savoy cafe, use of which was granted free by the proprietor, William Burgess. As no fee was paid for use of the building, no, responsible officers of the organization needed to be elected. If future gatherings are held in a public hall which is rented, an executive would have to be elected. This is understood to be the object of the chief of police, so that if future meetings contained statements which bordered on sedition there would be persons to hold responsible.
That is a most extraordinary statement. It is a most extraordinary condition of affairs when a chief of police undertakes to interfere with a private meeting held in a -private hall and insists that there -must be organized a society so that he can hold some society responsible for what is said. Sedition is not that kind of crime. It is the individual who commits sedition, if. sedition is committed, and it is the individual who should be charged. If this magistrate were guilty of sedition, the police might have arrested -and changed him *with sedition, but the idea of banning a meeting in a private hall or -cafe 'because it was not held under the auspices of some society just illustrates the ridiculous length to which some of our police are going. It reminds me of a motto which was hung up in the office of an editor of a paper in the western states at the time of the war: "We are 100 per cent Americans, so keep your mouth shut." In fact I fancy we are simply -copying some of the methods of the United States, and we ourselves are becoming somewhat infected by the hysteria that has prevailed so long on the other side of the line. I should like to call to the attention of hon. members and to commend this editorial which appeared yesterday in the Ottawa Journal and which deals with the communists:
Doesn't it all suggest that a lot of this talk about communists in Canada is inspired by fright, with the fright a product of ignorance, and that, taken together, the two things are hardly creditable to the country?
A little bit further on it states:
This country doesn't want to become another United States. Over there they have got to thinking that every, man who dares to express an original idea must necessarily be a com-

munist, if not an anarchist, so much so that they have made talk a crime, and have punished people for saying things that men like Jefferson would have thought mild. It will be far better for Canada if, in these matters, we stand by the old British way.
I heartily subscribe to that. This is a clipping of several years ago from a Toronto Star editorial and it is along the same lines:
How did England handle her affairs on May day? London is a wise old town, with a very long history. She has seen centuries and generations go by and from them has learned much. In most countries riots are spoken of and dealt with as revolutions. In England, revolutions, try as they may, can never palm themselves off as anything better than riots.
And so on.
There is much to be learned in this country from the way England deals with some things 

guided by an experience gained over a long period.
It would seem as if we on this continent were in a period similar to that through which England passed over one hundred years ago. The other day I was looking up May's Constitutional History and I noticed away back in 1792 the situation then was described as follows:
The government invested the doings of a small knot of democrats-chiefly workingmen- with the dignity of a widespread conspiracy to overturn the constitution. Ruling over a free state, they learned to dread the people, in the spirit of tyrants. Instead of relying upon the sober judgment of the country, they appealed to its fears; and in repressing seditious practices, they were prepared to sacrifice liberty of opinion. Their policy, dictated by the circumstances of a time of strange and untried danger, was approved by the prevailing sentiment of their contemporaries; but has not been justified in an age of greater freedom, by the maturer judgment of posterity.
I should like to come to this amendment. It is very limited in scope. I admit that it will not touch many of the abuses which I have mentioned to-night. It has really nothing to do with sedition. Sedition is dealt with under an altogether different clause in the code. My amendment is intended simply to clarify and safeguard the law with regard to unlawful assembly. The main clause of the law as it now stands in the criminal code, section 87 reads:
An unlawful assembly is an assembly of three or more persons who, with intent to carry out any common purpose, assemble in such a manner or so conduct themselves when assembled as to cause persons in the neighborhood of such assembly to fear, on reasonable grounds, that the persons so assembled will disturb the peace tumultuously or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to disturb the peace tumultuously.

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
I would add this amendment which has the effect of safeguarding the general right to assemble:
Nothing in this section shall restrict or interfere with the right of all persons peacefully to assemble for the purpose of discussing or hearing any discussion upon any matter of public interest, and such persons when so assembled shall not become an unlawful assembly merely by reason of speeches made to them or discussion carried on by them unless-
Then I think I add sufficient safeguards:
[DOT]-unless the general nature and character of such speeches or discussion would be likely, in the opinion of firm and reasonable persons, to cause an immediate breach of the peace.
The police in the instance to which I have referred were not able to prove that there was any likelihood that there would be caused an immediate breach of the peace. They simply did not like the particular group of people and they said that they could not hold a meeting and that if a meeting was held, it would be called an unlawful assembly, An assembly ought not to be called unlawful unless there would be an immediate breach of the peace. That is clearly the intention of the law. Further, whether or not this assembly would be unlawful, is to be judged not by the utterance of a single word, but rather by the nature and character of such speeches. I think that is the rule that is generally applied: that you are not to judge a man by some isolated word he may use; you must base your judgment upon the general nature and character of the speeches. I may say, for the benefit of my lawyer friends who may be interested, that that phrasing is in accord with the words used in the summing up of the judge in the case of Rex vs. Burns,
16 Cox C.C. 355.
Further:
Such speeches or discussion would be likely, in the opinion of firm and reasonable persons-
I do not know whether you can find those firm and reasonable persons in Toronto, although I would make an exception in the case of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Geary), who is sitting opposite. I am quite willing to trust myself in his hands. But when it comes to some of those who are on the bench or the police force, I am not very sure that I should feel that I could so entrust myself. I might say that this phrase, "firm and reasonable persons" is an almost verbatim reproduction of a phrase used in the judgment in the leading case of Rex vs. Vincent, which is cited in Crankshaws's Criminal Code, fifth edition, pages 108-109.
I do not think it is necessary for me to add anything to the case which I have pre-sentedi. Let me repeat that this amendment
22110-82	REVISED
has nothing whatever to do with sedition, and that it is very limited in its scope. It seeks simply to prevent some of the abuses which have grown up in the last few months, owing largely, I think, to ignorance and hysteria on the part of certain individuals in this country. As the side note to the bill states, and I cannot put it in better words, it is intended simply to provide a safeguarding clause to ensure that the general nature and character of speeches upon public affairs must be the ground for regarding any meeting unlawful. I cannot very well see, Mr. Speaker, how the house can refuse to accept an amendment of this character.
Mr. R. B. HANSON" (York-Sunbury):	I
desire to make a few brief observations on the subject matter of this bill. I impute no improper motives to the hon. gentleman who has fathered this proposed legislation (Mr. Woodsworth). He has stated to us that the amendment is very limited in its scope, and that it is his desire to clarify and to safeguard the law as it now stands. I submit to you, sir, and to the hon. members of this house, that the law as it now stands is perfectly clear and needs no clarifying, and further, that the privileges of any honest citizen in this country are to-day amply safeguarded under the existing provisions of the criminal code.
In my humble opinion the hon. gentleman has come to the wrong jurisdiction tO' attain the end which he has in view. I listened attentively to him and his plea, his indictment, if I may so call it, is not against the law as it stands on the statute books to-day, but against the manner in which that law is carried out by those who are charged with the responsibility of administering it. May I remind him most respectively that the parliament of Canada is not charged with the responsibility of administering the criminal law. That responsibility rests solely upon the provincial jurisdiction, and it is to those jurisdictions that the hon. gentleman and those associated with him should address themselves on this subject.
I hold no brief for the police force of the city of Toronto, but if I had to make a decision, I would say very frankly mat I am on the side of the police, and such I am sure would be the view of all thoughtful men in this assembly to-night. What is the law? The hon. gentleman has read the first part of section 87 of the criminal code relating to this matter, as follows:'
An unlawful assembly is an assembly of three or more persons who, with intent to carry out any common purpose-[DOT]
The intent, I remark, is an integral element of the offence:

speechtext:
1278 [DOT]	COMMONS

-assembles in such a manner or so conduct themselves when assembled as to cause persons in the neighborhood of such assembly to fear, on reasonable grounds, that the persons so assembled will disturb the peace tumultuously, or will by such assembly needlessly and without any reasonable occasion provoke other persons to disturb the peace tumultuously.
I admit frankly that it is often very difficult, sometimes impossible, to prove the intent with which people may assemble together. The intent may develop only after they have assembled and have spoken, and after they have caused the damage which is sought to be prevented. To limit the law in any way, to restrict it-not to use the word "clarify"-to restrict the law even in the very mild manner suggested by the hon. gentle-[DOT]man would be, I feel, to take away from those charged with the duty and responsibility and obligation of preserving the peace in this country some of the powers which they now have and upon which they must lean in the discharge of their duty.
I suggest to the hon. gentleman that his proposed amendment will in no event meet the situation which he apparently desires to meet. But even if he did take away some of their present powers from the police of this country, is it desirable in this time of unrest that the arm of the law be weakened rather than strengthened? I think we should pause before we do anything of a legislative character in this house which would have the effect of saying to those charged with the responsibility of administering the law: This you shall do, and this you shall not do. If the present law is too stringent, the hon. gentleman desires it to be ameliorated on the part of those who desire'-what? After all, what do those people in Toronto desire? I have not been present at their meetings and I have not heard directly what they do desire, but if I understand correctly from those who have been present and have reported their proceedings, the hand of these people is against established authority in this country. That is what it is; and would it not be a pretty spectacle in this year 1081 if parliament were to weaken the arm of the law which is to protect your home and mine, your family and mine? Certainly I am against anything that would tend toward the weakening of the authority of those charged with the responsibility of maintaining law and order. The onus in every case of proving a violation of the law is upon those who allege the law to have been violated, upon those who seek to punish someone charged with its violation; and if the chief of police of the city of Toronto or some other large municipality, having a direct
TMr. R. B. Hanson.)]
sense of the responsibility that rests upon him, has forbidden the holding of certain public meetings, is it not fair for hon. members to assume that he has reasonable grounds for his attitude, reasonable grounds to believe that there will be a breach of the peace? After all, the police must be the judge. I submit that parliament, having heard the few isolated instances that were related to the house by the promoter of the bill, and knowing perhaps none of the circumstances surrounding a single one of these cases-I submit that the hon. member himself cannot have any firsthand information, no information other than what he has gleaned from the newspapers- should not assume the responsibility of weakening the position of those in authority. Not for one minute do I believe that the members of this house will be so forgetful of their responsibility to our citizenship as to do anything of that sort, even in a negative manner; because I submit, and shall presently argue, that the proposed amendment is negative in itself and will have no force and effect.
What the hon. gentleman seeks to accomplish by 'his proposed amendment is now, I submit, the law of this country. That being so, the bill itself is wholly unnecessary. What is the affirmative part of the bill? He proposes to add the following subsection to section 87 of the criminal code:
Nothing in this section shall restrict or interfere with the right of all persons peacefully to assemble for the purpose of discussing or hearing any discussion upon any matter of public interest-
That is the law to-day, it always has been, and I hope if always will be, and there is no need to put upon the statute books any affirmative assertion such as is contained in what I have read. The proposed clause continues :
-and such persons when so assembled shall not become an unlawful assembly merely by reason of speeches made to them or discussion carried on by them-
Men must do much more than merely listen to speeches before they come within the purview of our criminal law. That is just what the law as it now stands provides for. Section 87 deals with intent, and I submit this is a very important element in the consideration of the question. It reads:
An unlawful assembly is an assembly of three or more persons who, with intent to carry out any common purpose, assemble in such a manner or so conduct themselves when assembled as to cause persons in the neighbourhood of such assembly to fear, on reasonable grounds,

Who are to be the judges of these grounds, -those making the speeches? Surely not.

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
Those in authority on the ground are charged with that responsibility and they must act, if, in their judgment on reasonable grounds, the position has become such that there is danger of a breach of the peace. I feel confident that this house will never do anything to impair the authority and power of those charged with that responsibility. The part of the amending clause that I have quoted, is, I submit, the criminal law of Canada to-day, and therefore this is wholly unnecessary. But the hon. gentleman, in language which apparently he has obtained from some legal decision, adds that there shall be no restriction-
[DOT]-unless the general nature and character of such speeches or discussion would be likely, in (he opinion of firm and reasonable persons, to cause an immediate breach of the peace.
" Immediate 'breach of the peace," that is to say, the hon. gentleman would lock the barn door after the horse is stolen-he would allow the people to meet, say anything they like, and after they have caused an "immediate breach of the peace" an indictable offence would be committed. In my opinion that is far too limited in its scope. We had better leave section 87 as it is, and not wait until there has been a breach of the peace before we bring those who assume that position within the ambit of the criminal law. I do not believe for a minute that on sober, calm reflection hon. members will be willing to vote for anything of that character.
Let me read very briefly what Roscoe in his work on criminal evidence says in regard to proof of unlawful assembly:
Proof of an unlawful assembly. Any meeting whatsoever, of great numbers of people, with such circumstances of terror as cannot but endanger the public peace, and raise fears and jealousies amongst the king's subjects, seems properly to be called an unlawful assembly.
If in the city of Toronto and in other places in the Dominion to which my hon. friend has referred the meetings which have been held there have not been of the character described by Roscoe, then I tell him there has been an excess of zeal on the part of those in authority. But that is no reason why this house should in a proper case take away from the authorities the power which is now theirs of acting properly within their discretion. Rather should my hon. friend, as I said a moment ago, appeal to those in authority over the police in the city of Toronto. I understand that the local police commission is composed of reputable men, first class citizens. Surely if my hon. friend has a good case he will not be denied a hearing in "Toronto the good." Surely they are not going to take away the liberty of
22110-82.}
the subject. What I fear is happening in Toronto, and is the desire of certain people there, is not liberty of speech but licence. If that be so, then I say, more power to the arm of the law, exercised with proper consideration and with reasonable care for the liberty of the subject.
For the reasons given, Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this bill. The law as it stands is quite clear, and in support of this I could cite judicial decisions from now till midnight, but I will not inflict them on the house. I submit there is no necessity to clarify the law, the liberty of the subject being already well safeguarded.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also am unalterably opposed to the amendment. I agree with my hon. friend from York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) that the provisions of the criminal code are quite adequate and do not involve any hardship on those who do not transgress them. The police authorities must enforce section 87 and the other provisions of the code. The right of every man to a fair trial has always been recognized under British institutions. As the section stands an unlawful assembly, or the members of it, would be charged with an indictable offence. That involves the right of trial by jury. As my hon. friend from York-Sunbury has said, in all criminal cases the burden of proof is on the crown. In other words, the accused is presumed to be innocent until the contrary is proven, and his guilt must be established beyond a reasonable doubt founded on the evidence What does my hon. friend propose? That an assembly shall not become an unlawful assembly:
-unless the general nature and character of such speeches or discussion would be likely, in the opinion of firm and reasonable persons, to cause an immediate breach of the peace.
Mark you, Mr. Speaker, an "immediate breach of the peace." If section 87 were so amended, men could assemble and as a matter of fact .cause a riot within five minutes. I say that this is a bad piece of legislation, to which I am unalterably opposed. We in New Brunswick do not seek legislation of this kind, and just here I should like to question the right of the hon. members for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) to speak on behalf of that great class of citizens, the labour element of Canada. I would far rather take the advice and counsel of such outstanding labour men in the province of New Brunswick as Mr. John S. Martin, former Labour member of the legislative assembly at Fredericton, or of Mr. Stanley S. Fleiger, of the town of Chatham, than that of my hon. friends opposite. The
1280	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
men I have mentioned, I submit, represent true Canadian labour; their judgment is sound and their capacity is unquestioned.
Just in conclusion let me say as a friend of labour, as one who had the high privilege of representing this great class in the courts of the land at the time of the strike in the lumber industry on the Miramichi river, about ten years ago, and as one who, as I feel, has received the wholehearted support of this great element in my county, that this bill does not commend itself to my labour friends in New Brunswick, and I for one am opposed to it. I invite hon. members on both sides of the house to come to a realization of the serious consequences of the proposed amendment. To me it seems to introduce a very radical and drastic change in our laws, and I submit that the law as it stands at the present time is adequate to preserve to our citizens the right to assemble for all lawful purposes.

subtopic: EDITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened with much attention to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), and 1 can assure him that as far as he is concerned he is perfectly safe in my hands in Toronto or elsewhere, , although I cannot say the same for his bill. As .other hon. members have said, my hon. friend directed his remarks rather to the administration of the criminal law, particularly with reference to its administration in Toronto, than to the substance of the law as we have it on the statute books. The hon. member read from section 87 of the criminal code the definition of an unlawful assembly, but I would call his attention to the next subsection of that same section, which goes on to say:
2. Persons lawfully assembled may become an unlawful assembly if they conduct themselves with a common purpose in such a manner .as would have made their assembling unlawful if they had assembled in that manner for that purpose.
I think that clearly indicates that there are and there can be, without any restriction of the law, meetings which are lawful, peaceful assemblies. That is to say, people may come together peacefully and lawfully, and may turn that meeting into an unlawful assembly by their conduct during the course of the meeting. Their conduct during the course of the meeting is not confined to physical conduct, gestures or anything like that, but I should say, embraces as well speaking and discussion, the manner of speaking and the manner of discussion. So when my hon. friend is introducing an amendment to provide that
[Mr. McDadej
people may come peacefully to a meeting, he is providing for something which is already provided for or implied by the statute as being already quite right and proper.
My hOn. friend has gone on in his bill to say that this peaceful or lawful meeting shall not become an unlawful assembly merely by reason of speeches made to that assembly or discussion carried on therein. In the explanatory note to the bill my hon. friend states, as he stated during the course of his remarks:
This bill is intended simply to provide a safeguarding clause to insure that the general nature and character of speeches upon public affairs must be the ground for regarding any meeting as unlawful.
If that is what the bill is designed to bring into effect, certainly it is not done by the measure proposed, which provides that you shall not call a meeting an unlawful assembly, or it shall not become an unlawful assembly, merely by reason of the speeches made. It may be an unlawful assembly for other reasons; as I say, under subsection 2 of section 87 it is provided in what ways a meeting may become unlawful, that is, by unlawful conduct including speeches.
I thoroughly agree with the two speakers who preceded me that there is nothing in this bill, with some exceptions to which I shall come in a moment, which carries the law one step further than it is at the present moment. There are certain points in the bill to which my attention is directed; the first is that the unlawful conduct must cause an immediate breach of the peace. There my hon. friend is making, from his point of view, a much less drastic bill than the code as it stands. Under the present code people at such meetings must conduct themselves so as to disturb the peace tumultuously, before the meeting can be termed an unlawful assembly. It would be more difficult to convict a person of attempting to disturb the peace tumultuously than of doing something which may provoke an immediate breach of the peace. But the introduction of the word "immediate" would indicate that, taking an extreme case, if somebody deliberately instructed people as to the preparation and use of bombs and as to the method to be followed the next day in using those bombs on some public building, certainly there would be a breach of the peace involved, but not occurring until the next day. My hon. friend, however, would say thac such a meeting was not unlawful because the breach of the peace which was provoked was not an immediate breach. Again, if we are to confine the unlawful conduct to speeches, no longer could one be convicted for any other

Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
method of agitation than that of the spoken word at a meeting.
I fear these words very greatly lessen the effect of the statute as it stands now, while getting my friend no further along the path which he seeks to tread, and for those reasons it seems to me the bill should not pass. In one view, the bill means nothing and so is unnecessary, and secondly there is the other reason that we do not know what the difficulty would be if, in order to convict, it had to be proved that the words were calculated to produce an immediate breach of the peace. In addition, my hon. friend provides in this bill that the nature and character of the speeches must be such as would have a certain effect on a "firm and reasonable person." I do not know such a class of persons in Toronto or anywhere else; they are not known to the law. My hon. friend is very much safer with the words of the section as they stand, which provide that the culpable conduct must be such as to cause persons in the neighbourhood to fear on reasonable grounds. That is the law as it stands now; reasonable grounds must be shown.
My hon. friend has outlined-and perhaps this is what brings me to my feet more than anything else-the history of certain happenings in the city of Toronto. The Board of Police Commissioners is not, of course, constituted under anything contained in the statutes of this parliament. As another hon. member said, it is independent of the city council and, so far as I know, the only restriction the city council is able to impose upon the actions of the board of police commissioners is that the board has to spend only the money the city council votes for that purpose, with this proviso, that the city council has nothing to say as to the number of policemen thought to be necessary for the preservation of law and order. That is a matter within the sole jurisdiction of the Board of Police Commissioners. I am not here to defend every action of the Board of Police Commissioners of Toronto, and I may say that in Toronto there has been a good deal of discussion as to whether that board under certain circumstances was right or not. They did pass two years ago some sort of order with reference to speeches made in other tongues than English, but I fancy it must be a dead letter. It would not appeal to me as a proper regulation to be in force, and if it is in force I can only say that I have sat time and again in meetings in Toronto where the speeches were delivered in some language other than English. I do not know what has
become of that regulation. I was not at home at the time of its discussion when it was first promulgated, but I should think it has become a dead letter, at least so far as my knowledge of it goes. .
With respect to this band of gentle idealists referred to by Saturday Night and known as the Toronto branch of the Fellowship of Reconciliation, the names of persons I have heard as belonging to it and interested in its *affairs are the names of very respectable citizens, and I do know that they had no end of a time with the Board of Police Commissioners. They were admitted to a hearing and were allowed to lay their charge and prove it if they could. About the beginning of the present year the present mayor, who became a member of the Board of Police Commissioners, undertook, with the assent of the other members of the board, to indicate the policy of that commission with regard to What is called free speech. The policy so enunciated by his worship has been generally accepted in the city of Toronto as being perfectly right: that is, that free speech, within the law and with proper respect for British institutions, British traditions and British principles, is the sort of speech that is to be allowed and encouraged in Toronto, as it probably is in every other part of the country. I mention this merely to show that if there was a misunderstanding as to what was thought by the police to be proper in the way of speech, the policy so enunciated by his worship the mayor, representing the Board of Police Commissioners, within the last two or three months, seems to have satisfied everyone as settling any controversy that had arisen.
There is no intimidation, I am advised by the Board of Police Commissioners, of the owners of halls as to what meetings they shall allow in those halls. The owner is responsible under the code for certain happenings, and he would remain so responsible under the amendment. There 'is no attempt to say to him whom he shall allow in his hall, what price he shall charge, or whether there shall be a licence for any meeting. I thought it well to clear up in the mind of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) the situation as it exists in Toronto and as I have indicated it.
So far as my city is concerned, my hon. friend need not concern himself very much. The people of Toronto are fully alive to the menace that lies in communism. They recognize that perhaps Toronto is the centre of communistic activity in Canada; at least,
I am told that Toronto is its headquarters.
1282	COMMONS
Criminal Code-Unlawful Assembly
The people of that city realize that and will . watch carefully. But they are not an unfair people; they do not propose to have the Board of Police Commissioners act outside the law. Neither do they wish to restrict in the least that freedom of speech so eloquently discussed by my hon. friend. Freedom of speech is not licence; it must be within the law-the law as it is laid down in the statute books or, it may be, the common law. And it is not asking too much, I think, when I ask the house to agree with me that freedom of speech must imply that those using that freedom are to use it with respect for British traditions, principles and institutions. That is what we are striving to enforce in Toronto. We are not troubled to any great extent in our administration, and any difficulty we have we believe we shall work out of satisfactorily.
I do not believe that on one construction this proposed section would add anything to the criminal law. On the other view, if we enact anything about the opinion "of firm and reasonable persons," something as to utterances that would cause an immediate breach of the peace, I do not know on what principles j'ou would direct the jury as to whether or not the onus had been proved or the defence made out. It would be introducing something new, something uncertain, to which I am not prepared to accede. For these reasons I do not believe that this bill should pass, and I shall vote accordingly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When the
house rose at six o'clock I was commenting on the Farm Loan. I stated that in 1927, the Liberal government of the day had a measure enacted so as to help the farmers to develop their farms by means of loans. I admire cur banking system. It has been rendering great services to our people. However, it will never answer the wishes or the needs of the farming classes, it was not established for that purpose, and the government realized that fact. Our farmers had to be assisted.
During the after-war depression, and the disorganisation of business which followed, formers availed themselves, extensively, of the Bankruptcy Act, which, was placed at their disposal to enrich certain people who were in that business, and laid hands on whatever assets the farmers might have, whereby the creditors and merchants, were left without anything on which to fall back. Many a time efforts were made and rightly so to amend

Agricultural Conditions
this act, I shall again refer to the subject shortly.
The Farm Loan Act was a new measure, it was possible to amend ancj improve it. It did not quite answer the end for which it was enacted. Among the reasons which prevented it being popular as it should have been, I shall point out three which should, at present, strongly appeal to the government. First, the 6J per cent rate is too high; secondly, the fees in connection with a loan are too high; thirdly, the 5 per cent required from the borrower, as board fund, does not appeal to the farmer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Who is responsible for this act? Who had it passed?
Some hon. MEMBERS (Translation): You
are responsible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I respectfully suggest that if the government-who have the interests of the farming classes at heart-wish sincerely to better the lot of farmers, there are other means than having subsidies of millions of dollars voted. There are certain considerations which must be kept in mind, and in this respect, I wish to make some suggestions. I shall willingly answer questions. There is an hon. member on the government benches who has a resolution on the orders of the day, the purport of which is to reduce the rate on interest from 6i per cent to 5 per cent. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Richmond-Wolfe (Mr. Lafleche) for his resolution. It meets my wishes and those of the entire country, and for this reason the government will probably accept it. This change has been asked in the past and it is also being requested this year. I personally make the same request. The provisions of the Act are known, they have been taken advantage of, if, however, they were made more easy they would become more, popular. This could be done by reducing the rate of interest from 6J per cent to 4 per cent, not 5 or 5^ per cent but 4 per cent.
It is true that the Quebec government, in its kindness and sdlicitude for the people, agreed to pay what should have been the federal government's share, nevertheless it still remains a Dominion Act. Have some pride, assume the responsibility of your act and take up your share of payments, in connection with legislation of which you should bear the burden, and Shoulder the whole responsibility.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You have. . .
Mr. VERVILLE (Translation). You may put that question in half an hour from now. Moreover, the fees necessary to obtain a loan are too high. I know this through experience because I am in the business.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: My services are free. That is why I am a poor man -and I wish to remain so-I give my services free to my fellow-citizens. The fees necessary to obtain a loan are too high I said. There are occasions when the board is most unreasonable in its demands and the farmers are unable to meet them. Let the government acquit these fees and strike out the clause which forces the borrower to pay 5 per cent on the amount loaned to him from the funds of the board. The farmer who borrows is not a lender, but a borrower and if he is required to contribute 5 per cent to the funds of the board, he strikes a bad bargain. Seeing that the government has established the Farm Loan Board to assist farmers, let them not follow the example of banks. It should not be looked upon as a paying business. The banks look after their interest, but the Farm Loan Board is a different institution, it is a government affair, it was enacted to help the farmer. Let us lend hkn a hand, and let us never demand from the farmer who borrows $5,000 to return 5 per cent of that amount.

These three considerations are the reason why the present act, although in force, is not as popular as it should be. Let the government, which made So many pledges which they cannot realize, adopt the amendment that I have suggested, it would be a splendid move.
Moreover, the Bankruptcy Act stands as an appendix to the previous act. The former is indeed a fine piece of legislation. Like many others, I ask-my only aim being to serve the farming community-that the farmers be deprived of the facility which is given them of having recourse to the Bankruptcy Act. In the past, our people called on their neighbours, their relatives or their friends, when they needed $500, $1,000 or $5,000, and they got it. Owing to after-war conditions and the present depression, no farmer is able to borrow $500, $200 not even $100 from a relative or friend; no one will advance him money. What contributed to ruin entirely the farmer's credit? Practically, it was the Bankruptcy Act. I do not wish to despoil it of its merits, for it serves its purpose. However, as far as the farmer is concerned, I ask the government-others have made that request-to withdraw from the farmer that opportunity which is afforded him of going into bankruptcy whenever he sees fit. That is what ruined his credit and forces him, at present, to beg from friends the bread needed at home.

speechtext:
There is
another question. Will our opponents-who claim to be the friend of the farming class- after being responsible for the conditions under which we live and of which the farmers bitterly complain, after their deceitful pledges, try to remedy these conditions by giving away millions of dollars. I well recall, just a few years past when we were in power, they strongly criticized our experimental farms. I shall explain: there are throughout the country large experimental farms which are very tiseful and fulfil the end for which they were established, they have already rendered great service to agriculture. I contend that this is the time to give this kind of farm education the greatest development and publicity. Instead of establishing experimental farms in each district let us utilize those already established for experimental purposes, and let us spread farm education by establishing demonstration farms -not one but many-so that all may benefit by them.
Are you aware that, in certain sections of the country, when' our farmers leave to visit these experimental farms, they act very much as if they were going to an Exhibition.
Educate our farming classes and give them the means to acquire useful knowledge. Do not oblige them to travel at much expense to themselves so as to enjoy a good dinner and see fine and healthy cattle; keep them on the farm, in their parishes if necessary, and teach them the knowledge they require, and this, at no expense to them. That was a ' policy advocated in the past by our opponents which they now forget to put into practice.

speechtext:
Pep, sir,
is the lot of youth. My friend will become wiser with years, if not his constituents may show some resentment for his interference. If the government is in earnest-which I doubt-they have something better to do than vote millions of dollars. The people have been suffering for the last nine months and they call for markets to sell their products. If, in assuming office Mr. Bennett closes all gates, the people will smash them, however, owing to the respect they have for law, they will bide their time. Give us markets, that is all we ask. You were put in office owing

to the extraordinary pledges you gave, you promised to make us happy, do so! You promised our farmers that they would sell their butter at 50 cents per pound, find them such a market. You equally promised them that they would sell their eggs from 35 to 40 cents per dozen, show them where they can get those prices, it is your duty.
At present, potatoes are sold $1.00 per bag; in the past they fetched $2.00; find them such a market. Those are pledges which were not kept, and there is no getting out of it. Stop dreaming and come back to earth. Protection has perhaps its good side, however, we are living in too critical a time to keep on dreaming. Face the facts. Our farmers demand markets for the sale of their products.
I do not wish to delay the house, however, there are questions that must be discussed and the house is the proper place to do so. I was asked on Saturday last by my constituents, why things were at a stand-still. My reply was: We are unable to make any progress, Mr. Bennett is in office, and Mr. Bennett is the government; forward your requests to the Prime Minister. May I, sir, give the same advice to everybody:	that in future all
requests should be made to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett). The people will no doubt request that all pledges be fulfilled. May I also, sir, console my constituents by telling them: Be courageous, live in hope. Perhaps this rule of terror will not last long and in a few years a good Liberal regime may replace the present one and prove satisfactory to you.
The Conservatives, sir, never let up talking of distrust and discouragement during their election campaign. They told the people: The King government is no good, banish it, place us in office, we will look after your interests. We will revive what seems dead. For sometime past however, things have been more than ever at a standstill. We also note that no pledges were kept. It behooves any one who has a policy to submit and represents his fellow citizens, to constantly inspire them with confidence. What happened last summer? Disillusion and distrust were continuously being referred to.
The most cherished thought which a public man can harbour, is that intimate assurance of having bettered the people and of having inspired them with confidence in the administrative order. If I respect the powers that be, -the king, the government which protects me-I have confidence in them. I clearly realize that this government forgets its mission when it preaches otherwise.
In closing my remarks, may I give an advice to the leader of the government, that is: to set aside all selfishness and walk hand

Agricultural Conditions
in hand with the people instead of dreaming, to efficiently govern the country, by keeping in touch with its needs; to be one of the people, help them and be of some service to them.
I shall end my speech by saying: Let us endeavour to have the people love what they should love. Let us tell them: love your country, love its administration,-though I realize they cannot love those who are now in power,.-love those in office when they are worthy of it, but in any case show respect for law and order.

speechtext:
I am in no
way complaining; but I would have been happy to see him here and I hope that tomorrow or in the course of the next few days he will acquaint himself with the speech just delivered by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Yerville), which speech levelled pointed, though quite justified, criticism at the preceding administration.
My hon. friend from Lotbiniere finds fault with the Farm Loan Act. He cannot reasonably claim that the present government has had time to change the act. When the hon. member complains that the farmer who borrows money must pay exorbitant rates everybody in the house understands that he is criticizing the adminstration of the former prime minister of this country.
When the hon. member for Lotbiniere speaks of our experimental farms and gives advice to the government, he is quite plainly criticizing the former regime, since the present government has not had time to make any changes as regards experimental farms. However, I can assure my hon. friend that such changes will be made before long; and thereafter our experimental farms will be of some use to agriculture.
I had no intention of taking part in the present debate; but so many contradictory, incomplete and even inaccurate statements have been made on the floor of this house that I felt it my duty as the representative of a farming constituency, to put matters in their proper light.
The hon. members of the opposition say that the price of butter has fallen very low. Quite so. Nobody denies that fact. But our friends on the other side of the house seek to lay the blame at the door of the present government. For this purpose the house has
been treated to certain statements which, I repeat what I said a moment ago, are inaccurate and incomplete; some are even contrary to the true state of affairs. For instance, Mr. Speaker, it was stated that Canada had imported 2,098,379 pounds of butter during the first three months of 1931. That is a fact. But to be fair to the government and make the case more complete our friends of the opposition should have made the comparison between the first three months of 1930 and the first three months of the present year. This comparison shows that Canada, during the first three months of the year 1930, imported 24,159,568 pounds of butter.
An hon. MEMBER (Translation):	This
year or last year?

At any rate, here are the facts: During the year ending March 31st, 1930, we imported 28,000,000 pounds of butter. During the year following our imports were
6.000.	000 pounds; but there is this further important detail that, out of the total of
6.000.	000 pounds, almost 5,000,000 entered Canada before the legislation passed at the emergency session last September came into force. That is the first point I wanted to clear up, Mr. Speaker.
But the matter does not end there. It must be borne in mind that, although butter is selling at a very low price just now, we ourselves are supplying Canada's requirements; our own Canadian producers are providing the butter needed by the Canadian consumer -something which had not happened, Mr. Speaker, since the notorious Australian treaty was negotiated by our friends to your left.
Agricultural Conditions

Neither should it be forgotten that our prices here are higher than in London, that they are still above the world level, and further that no more butter is entering Canada from New Zealand. This latter source, practically inexhaustible, which caused such havoc in the eastern townships, need worry us no longer. We are receiving only a few pounds of butter from Australia.
The hon. member for St. Henri stated on the floor of the house tbait promises had been made to the effect that no more butter would be imported into Canada from across the sea. I do not know whether he himself heard any such promises made. People are prone to some exaggeration at election time. I may tell him in reply that I made no such promises. I was well aware that a contract existed between Canada and Australia, and that we had to live up to that contract. I understand that next summer representatives of the Australian Commonwealth are coming to Canada and that our ministers will avail themselves of the opportunity thus afforded to negotiate a new treaty, a new contract. Meanwhile we are bound by the contract entered into by our friends on the other side of the House.
That is about all I had to say on this much-discussed butter question. I want to emphasize to the house that since the legislation of last September came into force our imports have been limited to some two million pounds of butter, while during the previous year we had received 28 million pounds. It is true some 4 millions came into the country during the three months immediately preceding the enacting of that legislation.
The legislation of the short session helped the farmers in another way. Now the farmers in the neighbourhood of cities can for the first time enjoy the benefits of their own markets and sell their early produce without fear of what almost amounts to unfair foreign competition, either from the United States or from the islands of the Atlantic. They are well pleased with the laws passed last September. I do not believe a single member coming from the neighbourhood of Montreal, and who has truck-gardeners among his constituents, would dare claim that these people who after all, make up a respectable and considerable portion of our farming community, are not delighted with the new laws which have proven so beneficial to them.
Mr. Speaker, I rose to point out the misapprehension which has arisen from the answers appearing on page 985 of Hansard, and which I thought needed a word of explanation, to forestall any interpretation contrary to fact.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few
words in reply to the two hon. members who preceded me. I want to point out to the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil), in spite of the insinuations he made against the butter trade and the wholesale houses in the city of Montreal, that when the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) was looking for enlightenment and advice he did not go to the farmers, but to these very merchants in Montreal.
It is easy to say that not much butter is coming into Canada at the present time, and that a lot came in last year; but after all, whether our imports are large or small, what interests our eastern township farmers is not the quantity of butter entering the country, but the price at which butter is selling here today. It is an absolute fact that last Monday butter was selling on the Montreal market for 22 cents a pound. It is also a fact that a year ago, when we were receiving such large quantities of butter from New Zealand and Australia, butter sold for 35 cents a pound.
For the benefit of my hon. friend from Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) I note that to-day, for the first time in ten years I believe, the price of butter is a little lower in Montreal than in London.
Another conviction of mine is that the farmer is entitled to a steady market, like other producers strive to attain. When we see the Government in power put a duty on potatoes one day and remove that duty two weeks later, it seems to me that the farmers can have no idea where they are going, nor can the merchants, nor the other citizens of Canada.
I shall add one further word in reply to the hon. gentleman from Stanstead concerning this much talked-of page 985 of Hansard. I have every confidence in my esteemed friend, but I do not believe he answered the question, nor did he point out one single falsehood on page 985. I think the figures in question are accurate. I would probably accept them in preference to a good many figures quoted by hon. members on the government side. Let me draw the atteniion of the hon. members for Compton and Stanstead to what I find on page 985-it is there for all to see: from August 1st, 1930 to March 1st, 1931 the present government collected a duty of 1 cent per pound on Australian butter. On 1074 we find that under the King government the tariff on this same butter was 1.70 cents per pound. So the present government is actually putting a lighter duty on Australian butter this year than we did.

And that, as my hon. friend from St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) noted a while ago, despite Conservative pledges that if returned to power they would put a stop to the imports of butter from New Zealand and Australia.

Mr. Speaker, I noticed that the speeches delivered by Conservatives during the election campaign were entirely different from those we now listen to in the house. During the election our opponents claimed that no reason could justify the low prices paid for farm products. I recall that they told us then, that if Mr. Bennett was elected on July 28, the farm products would sell at a much higher price. I also recall asking my opponent in the riding of 1'Islet: How could Mr. Bennett increase the prices and negotiate favourable trade treaties with other countries, with a protective policy like the one he wishes to inaugurate in this country? His answer was: Mr. Bennett will blast open markets. I also, inquired: What means would Mr. Bennett take to increase the price of butter and the production of milk? His answer was: Mr. Bennett will seize the bull by the horns. I had never heard, sir, of such a policy, and I frankly admit that I was anxious to be present at the emergency session, so as to witness on the flour of the house these new dynamiters, these political toreadors who seize the bull by the horns. I confess I was somewhat disappointed. Once here, I perceived that these great statesmen had very little to say.
I listened to the hon. member for Mont-magny (Mr. LaVengne) during the election. He then proclaimed that 'he would see to it that the price of butter increased. Furthermore, he promised that 'the factories of Mont-magny would open their doors and give work to about 1,500 people, thus creating a market to help the farmers and should the doors remain closed, he pledged himself to give up his mandate. I notice that he has shifted his aim, he no more endeavours to have 'the doors of the Montmagny mills opened but is bent on having the name of Dominion of Canada changed to the Kingdom of Canada-this will be of great benefit to the farming class of Montmagny.
I also listened to the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve). He established a record in the last July elections by his eloquence. He carried Two Mountains without assistance, but once in the house no mention of agriculture is made. He does not even refer to the growing of couch-grass Which he advocated when leader of the opposition in Quebec.

speechtext:
Let us drop the subject. This government has done nothing for the farming class. What hon. members endeavour to prove is that during the Liberal regime 28,000,000 pounds of butter were imported from New Zealand or Australia, while this year only 6,000,000 pounds were imported. What interests the farmers is not so much the quantity imported from Australia, but the price they get for their butter. They were haippier when they received, on July 28, 30 cents for their 'butter than they are to-day.
The $20,000,000 appropriated to relieve unemployment were of no benefit to rural districts because municipalities were too poor to take advantage of it, that is, to pay their quota. This means that the rural districts will be called upon to contribute their quota of this appropriation without having benefited by it through the identity card which means telling the farmers: you will be given no work as a means of earning your share of the $20,000,000, but you will be taxed for it all the same.
The repairs to wharfs in my county and that of Montmagny, for which appropriations had been voted by the house, were not carried out, this would, indeed, have been a great help to the farmers of our ridings. On the other hand, $2,000,000 were spent on the Welland canal without being not voted by the house.
I state, sir, that two-thirds of the money appropriated for public works in Quebec was not spent. In brief, there was no need to call a special session, there was no need of federal help to alleviate unemployment. The government had but one thing to do, that is, apply the money which was voted for public works in our counties. The government made a great stir over that $20,000,000, and proclaimed that, thanks to it, much suffering had been avoided throughout the country; yet, this year when conditions are 50 per cent worse, when unemployment has increased 50 per cent, that same government cuts off $38,000,000 from the estimates.
This is not rational, sir, or else I am greatly mistaken. $20,000,000 more last year to relieve unemployment, and when conditions are worse this year, $38,000,000 less toward relieving unemployment. Two million dollars is given to

the city of Quebec to alleviate unemployment while one million is withdrawn also to alleviate unemployment.
The farmers, sir, are already aware of the deceitful policy of this government, this money was of no benefit to them and they realize now that they will be taxed to the tune of $20,000,000. Through its tariff policy, the government has closed foreign markets to Canadian products and has increased the price of manufactured goods which the farmer is bound to purchase. In other words the farmer sells his products for almost nothing while he pays a very high price for what he needs. Take, for instance, the price of butter, it lent itself to much controversy and the hon. member for Compton, although deploring that butter was so cheap, seemed to assure us that the farmer was satisfied.

I have here
souvenirs of the last election. There was a great deal of this fine campaign literature distributed all over the country. Here is a pamphlet from Conservative headquarters in which it is stated that the cost of butter production in Canada, according to experts of Macdonald College, is 39 cents per pound. So that, at present, for each pound of butter produced the farmer loses 17 cents. In the face of such distressing conditions and especially after the speeches to which we listened in the course of the last election, I thought that the government would feel very depressed and that the Prime Minister would be in his seat to hear, at least, the hon. member for Compton. No one seems to care. The hon. Minister of Agriculture, himself, is as silent as a tombstone which lies in a grave yard of broken election pledges. When information is requested, what answers do we get? None. What information was I able to gather in regard to agriculture in my constituency? 1 was able to lay my hands on a document, " Bull Loaning Policy " that is all I found in it. On the first page, is seen a bull without horns. It is certainly not the government's bull which the Prime Minister was to seize by the horns, according to my opponent.
The farming class received nothing from the federal government and the farmers would be in great distress, in Quebec, had it not been for the provincial government's help. To give you an idea of the outlay made to help the farmers in our rural districts, let me point out that in the counties of 1'Islet and Kamou-raska, in connection with roads only, the

Agricultural Conditions
provincial government spent $329,000. For colonization purposes we are granted between $20,000 to $25,000 per year. Apart from this, the provincial government provide funds for the building of schools, up to an amount of $1,200 per year for each school so as to help primary education in rural districts. Those amounts just mentioned were given to help the farmers of l'lslet and Kamouraska; thanks to these grants we were able to face the present crisis. This is mot all that the provincial government has done. I know that, this year, in the newly settled districts of Kamouraska, Mont-magny and llslet, the provincial government had seed grain distributed free. This is how our provincial government administer the affairs of the province. I recall having seen, at the last session, in Quebec, grants given to those who wished to drain and break their land. I know that this is a policy that many approve, and I feel certain that the hon. member for Two Mountains (Mr. Sauve), who has always favoured agriculture, certainly approves of the measures advocated this year.
We have done a great deal, in Quebec, to help agriculture. Take, for instance, the riding of my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard), you will find there an experimental farm which was established in that county when that riding was represented in this house by the hon. Mr. Lapointe. I think, that this experimental farm is one of the first established, in the Quebec district at any rate. It is under Dominion control, admirably well managed by a man who is deserving of all our congratulations. This institution simply aims at spreading new farming methods and does not look forward to returns, but it is continuously experimenting for the benefit of the farmers. The government, however, .found that while this experimenting has its good points, the farmers could hardly obtain the necessary information and keep tab on the experiments tried in these agricultural schools. The system, therefore, of demonstration farms was resorted to in all the rural districts. These demonstration farms duplicate the experiments carried out on experimental farms in the presence of the farmer who is able to benefit by them. '
We also have an agricultural college at Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere. That is probably why we have as representative of Kamouraska one of the best scientific agriculturists of the province of Quebec. May I mention also that, this year, the. agricultural college was not forgotten. Our Quebec farmers are not so much behind the times as some may think. The Quebec government appropriated, this year, $200,000 for the agricultural college of Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere.

Who was the first, in Quebec, to foster the education of numerous agriculturists? It was the hon. Joseph-Edouard Caron, who loved farming, and had many a battle with the hon. member for Two Mountains. However, I think, that both worked to attain the same end because they were always very good friends.

We did not
fight, we discussed seriously.
