speechtext:
The hon.
Postmaster never fights. Although his fight was successful on July 28.
They trained a group of agriculturists who are now spread throughout the rural counties of Quebec. These men are destined to render great services to the farming dass. Not only do they teach scientific methods to farmers but they are well qualified to follow experiments which take place at experimental farms, they are there to see that the farmers of the various counties receive the grants made by Liberal or Conservative governments, they endeavour to teach the farmer and impress on him that there is always a market, especially for standardized farm products. Moreover, sir, these agricultural experts are found in every county, whether liberal or conservative, organizing farming competitions which are most useful to agriculture, as they stimulate and create a certain friendly intercourse between the leading farmers of various counties; and the young men take an interest in these demonstrations.
I know, sir, that everybody is, indeed, prompted by the same motives and is desirous of helping the farming class. We, from Quebec, have much sympathy with the citizens of the west in these difficult times. They can rest assured that we greatly sympathize with them in their present day trials. We have our own troubles and we hope to overcome them, thanks to the energy which characterizes the farmers of Quebec.
One suggestion I would like to make to the house. It is the fostering of small industries in our rural districts in order to decentralize industrial towns. There is an excellent instance of this decentralization in my county. In my native parish there exists an industry known as the L'lslet Foundry which specializes in stoves, heating system equipment and baths with an up-to-date enamel factory attached thereto. Thanks to this industry, the neighbouring parishes of llslet send the surplus of their population to these factories which gives them an opportunity to earn an honest living.
One hears a great deal about the advantages of our banking system. My connection with banks is not sufficiently extensive to consider
Agricultural Conditions

myself as a banking expert. Generally, when I deal with banks it is to negotiate a loan. I acknowledge that our banking system is a safe one but it also claims all the savings of our rural population, centralizing them in large cities-I noticed that in the United States- I do not like to quote the United States as an example or to copy their institutions, because I believe that our banking system is superior to theirs-I noticed, however, in the United States a banking system established with the aim of assisting the depositors and encouraging local industries. The depositor receives a reasonable interest for 'his money, however, what is most noticeable, is that banks cannot make loans outside of certain specified districts. That is, in a district like the counties of l'lslet and Montmagny, for instance, the banks would accept the savings of farmers, pay them 5 per cent on their deposits and the money could not be loaned outside the counties of l'lslet and Montmagny. This system would work splendidly here, because our farmers could place their savings-when they have any-with a sound banking institution, and feel assured that such funds will be used in industries known to them. This would prove a boon to our farmers, especially after the poor investments which have been made for some time past. I can state that within the last two years, in PIslet alone, S200.000 were lost in unprofitable investments. This represents the savings of, at least, two generations. Widows and heads of large families, who had with difficulty realized savings, were, in the space of a few weeks, ruined by swindlers who have the gift of convincing honest people to invest money in their schemes.

speechtext: The members on this side of the house are outspoken. I shall give you my views on the Russian embargo. Everyone in this house, whether French or English Canadian, Protestant or Catholic, are absolutely opposed to the policy prevailing in Russia. Everybody is opposed to such a policy.

Russian policy, but the embargo.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE

The hon. member is well informed: he thinks that bolshevism comes with coal. He intends to tell us that the Russian embargo is a splendid act of the government. He was not a member of this house when we were in office and the right hon. Mr. Mackenzie King moved the embargo on alcohol. This, sir, was a shock to the gentlemen on your right; still it was not to be compared with the Russian embargo. Notwithstanding this, England buys Russian wheat, and will continue to do so, she will purchase hats from Russia and stick the label "Made in England;" the Compton people will buy those hats. Instead of settling Russian affairs, let us settle ours, those of Canada.
You have as Prime Minister of Saskatchewan one of your friends whose policy is worse than that holding sway in Russia. The exodus of our people towards the United States has been referred to. It is therefore not to be wondered at, if French-Canadians instead of settling in Saskatchewan, where they are not allowed to speak their language, or even kneel down,

barely are they allowed to bring up a family,-should take the road which leads to the United States, where at least they are given hospitality. In what country are we living? I was in the United States, at Easter, visiting the beautiful city of Manchester. Who says that Canadians do not amount to much

Business of the House
in the United States? The mayor of Manchester, a city half English and half French, was a Mr. Moreau and he is a credit to that city. Travel through Massachusetts and visit the towns of Springfield and Holyoke; both at their city halls and their banks you will find French-Canadians in charge. Three weeks ago, I attended mass at Barry, in Vermont, and to my great surprise the priest, an Irishman whose French was somewhat deficient, was not ashamed to give his instructions and preach in both French and English. In leaving the church I wondered why in our own country, in Saskatchewan, the children were not allowed to learn their own language and practise their religion. Yet, it was the French-Canadian race that sent out the first pioneers and settlers to that western country. When comparing conditions, I thought to myself: We are worse off than they are in Russia.
I see, sir, that my time is almost up. I wish, in closing my remarks, to state that I am acquainted with what is going on in Quebec, I know the feelings of our rural districts, I also have some knowledge of the feelings which exist in cities, and if it is true to say that the Tory government has a majority to rule over us, it is also true to state that it is always liberalism which rules in the people's hearts.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Wednesday, May 6, 1931.
